evidence.quote: Compared with unassisted manual review, the LLM-assisted workflow improved accuracy (F1 = 0.88 vs 0.77), inter-rater agreement measured by Cohen's kappa (kappa = 0.82 vs 0.50), and reduced average review time by approximately half.

evidence.title: Prompting is not enough: supervised baselines and leakage control for measuring shared decision-making with LLMs in pediatric encounters
evidence.outcome: Macro kappa of zero-shot LLM versus simpler supervised classifier on the same data
evidence.effect: Zero-shot LLM macro kappa 0.139 (95% CI 0.111-0.164) vs supervised classifier 0.227 (0.186-0.262); paired improvement 0.088 (0.051-0.119); stack 0.242.
evidence.quote: The supervised classifier reached kappa = 0.227 (0.186-0.262), a paired improvement of 0.088 (0.051-0.119).

evidence.title: Development and Feasibility Evaluation of an Edge AI as Medical Device System for Breast Cancer Multidisciplinary Team Meetings
evidence.outcome: Treatment recommendation accuracy and concordant interventions versus proprietary cloud comparator
evidence.effect: MedGemma-RAG identified 2.3 times more MDT-concordant interventions than the proprietary cloud comparator (p = 0.020), with no significant difference in overall accuracy.
evidence.quote: MedGemma-RAG identified 2.3 times more MDT-concordant interventions than a proprietary cloud comparator (p = 0.020), with no significant difference in overall accuracy.

evidence.title: Improving O-RADS Risk Stratification from Ultrasound Reports: A Comparative Evaluation of Hybrid versus End-to-End LLM Reasoning Strategies
evidence.outcome: O-RADS classification accuracy of LLM strategies versus original clinical reports against expert consensus
evidence.effect: Hybrid Gemini 3.6 Flash accuracy 99.2% (387/390) vs original clinical reports 87.7% (342/390) and end-to-end LLM strategies 65.6% to 95.9%.
evidence.quote: Its performance surpassed that of original clinical reports (accuracy, 87.7% [342 of 390]; weighted kappa = 0.94; 95% CI: 0.91-0.96) and end-to-end LLM strategies (accuracy range, 65.6% [256 of 390] to 95.9% [374 of 390]).

evidence.title: Automated Chest CT Protocol Selection via Large Language Model Derived Text Embeddings from Imaging Request Text
evidence.outcome: LLM protocol accuracy versus radiologists on 300 cases with expert consensus
evidence.effect: LLM overall accuracy 80% versus 83% for radiologists, no significant difference (p = 0.263); LLM exceeded radiologists for some challenging categories.
evidence.quote: On 300 independent cases with expert consensus, the LLM reached an overall accuracy of 80% versus 83% for radiologists, with no significant difference (p = 0.263).

evidence.title: Large Language Models Versus Physicians in Traditional Chinese Medicine: A Real-World Clinical Case Evaluation
evidence.outcome: Expert scores of LLMs versus TCM physicians on same outpatient cases
evidence.effect: Cutting-edge general-purpose LLMs achieved higher expert scores than the 60 physician comparators, especially for medical advice, treatment principles and selected diagnostic tasks.
evidence.quote: Cutting-edge general-purpose LLMs achieved higher expert scores than the physician comparators, particularly for medical advice, treatment principles and selected diagnostic tasks.
evidence.sample_unit: cases (de-identified outpatient TCM cases; 16 LLMs and 60 physicians compared)

evidence.title: Large-Language-Model Mortality Risk Stratification in the Intensive Care Unit: A Benchmark Against APACHE II
evidence.outcome: LLM mortality risk stratification compared with APACHE II
evidence.effect: LLMs classified more patients as high risk than APACHE II, with calibration mismatch; Gemini with added context uniquely identified a low-risk group.
evidence.quote: LLMs demonstrated a general tendency toward risk overestimation, classifying more patients as high risk compared to APACHE II.

evidence.title: Artificial Intelligence (AI) Assisted Decision Making in Malignant Pleural Mesothelioma: A Comparative Study of AI Responses
evidence.outcome: Likert-scored LLM treatment recommendations versus multidisciplinary tumor board decisions across three LLMs
evidence.effect: ChatGPT mean 4.50 ± 0.57 vs Gemini 3.77 ± 0.43 and Copilot 3.85 ± 0.52 (p < 0.001); performance differed substantially between candidate tools.
evidence.quote: ChatGPT demonstrated superior performance with the highest mean score (4.50 ± 0.57) and a median score of 5, significantly outperforming Gemini (mean 3.77 ± 0.43, median 4) and Copilot (mean 3.85 ± 0.52, median 4) (p < 0.001).
evidence.sample_unit: questions (12 cases x 5 questions per LLM)

evidence.title: From Tool to Teammate: A Randomized Controlled Trial of Clinician-AI Collaborative Workflows for Diagnosis
evidence.outcome: diagnostic accuracy versus traditional resources
evidence.quote: Clinicians using either collaborative workflow outperformed those using traditional tools, achieving average accuracies of 85% (AI-first) and 82% (AI-second), compared to 75% with traditional resources (p < 0.0004 and p < 0.00001; mean differences = 9.8% and 6.8%; 95% CI = 4.6%–15% and 4.0%–9.6%).

evidence.title: Enhancing Privacy-Preserving Deployable Large Language Models for Perioperative Complication Detection: A Targeted Strategy with LoRA Fine-tuning
evidence.outcome: AI model performance for perioperative complication detection compared with human experts on same records
evidence.effect: State-of-the-art models consistently outperformed human experts; fine-tuned 4B model F1 rose from 0.18 to 0.55 versus human experts' F1=0.526; 8B model F1>0.61.
evidence.quote: Initial evaluations revealed that state-of-the-art models consistently outperformed human experts, particularly reasoning models.

evidence.title: Large Language Models Improve Coding Accuracy and Reimbursement in a Neonatal Intensive Care Unit
evidence.outcome: Diagnostic accuracy of candidate LLMs versus human coders on the same NICU notes, physician-adjudicated
evidence.effect: GPT-o3-mini 79.1% vs human coders 76.3% (P=.52); GPT-4o 58.6% (P<.001 vs both), so the comparison separated a comparable model from an underperforming one.
evidence.quote: GPT-4o underperformed at 58.6% (95% CI, 52.5%-64.7%; P < .001 vs both).

evidence.title: Toward the Autonomous AI Doctor: Quantitative Benchmarking of an Autonomous Agentic AI Versus Board-Certified Clinicians in a Real World Setting
evidence.outcome: AI diagnostic and treatment concordance versus board-certified clinicians on same encounters
evidence.effect: Top diagnosis matched in 81% of cases; treatment plan aligned in 99.2%; in discordant cases AI superior in 36.1%, human superior in 9.3%.
evidence.quote: The top diagnosis of Doctronic and clinician matched in 81% of cases, and the treatment plan aligned in 99.2% of cases.

evidence.title: Responsible AI in Action: Planning through Implementation of a Mortality Model for Palliative Care
evidence.outcome: Comparison of new model against existing commercial model on the same data
evidence.effect: SICLI outperformed the commercial EOLCI on the same cohort: AUC 0.87 vs 0.81.
evidence.quote: SICLI was very well calibrated and outperformed the EOLCI (AUC of 0.87 (95% CI:0.86, 0.87) vs. 0.81, (95% CI: (0.80, 0.81)).

evidence.title: Physician- versus Large Language Model-Generated Clinical Summaries in the Emergency Department
evidence.outcome: Comparison of LLM-generated versus physician-authored ED one-liner summaries on accuracy, completeness, utility
evidence.effect: LLM summaries rated higher: accuracy 4.18 vs 3.40 (β=0.78, p<.001); completeness 3.69 vs 3.25 (p=.005); utility 3.88 vs 3.21 (p<.001). LLM preferred in 50.5% of encounters, physician in 38.4%.
evidence.quote: Across all dimensions, LLM-generated summaries received higher ratings than physician-authored summaries.

evidence.title: How Good Are Large Language Models at Supporting Frontline Healthcare Workers in Low-Resource Settings – A Benchmarking Study & Dataset
evidence.outcome: Expert-rated response quality of LLMs versus local clinicians on 11 metrics
evidence.effect: All LLMs significantly outperformed local clinicians (ps < 0.001) across all metrics; Gemini-2 surpassed local GPs by an average of 0.83 points (range 0.38-1.10).
evidence.quote: All LLMs significantly outperformed local clinicians (ps < 0.001) across all metrics, with Gemini-2, for example, surpassing local GPs by an average of 0.83 points on every metric (range: 0.38 – 1.10).

evidence.title: Assessing ChatGPT-4 as a Clinical Decision Support Tool in Neuro-Oncology Radiotherapy: A Prospective Comparative Study
evidence.outcome: ChatGPT-4 radiotherapy recommendations versus tumor board, independent specialist, and guidelines on same cases
evidence.effect: ChatGPT-4 agreed with tumor board in 76% (κ=0.61) and with independent specialist in 79%; specialist overall agreement was 90%; AI showed overtreatment bias (p<0.05).
evidence.quote: Its overall agreement (76%) was lower than that of the human specialist (90%).

evidence.title: CardiacGPT™: A Real-Time AI Assistant for Intraoperative Guidance and Postoperative Decision Support in Cardiac Surgery
evidence.outcome: Clinician trust ratings of four candidate LLMs on the same 500 cardiac surgery cases
evidence.effect: GPT-5 mean 4.83 and Claude 3.5 Opus 4.79 (each >98% high-trust); Sonnet 3.9 (74%); Haiku 3.6 (66%). Side-by-side comparison exposed clear differences between candidate models.
evidence.quote: Claude 3.5 Sonnet performed moderately (mean 3.9, 74% high-trust), while Claude 3.5 Haiku produced less context-specific recommendations (mean 3.6, 66% high-trust).
evidence.sample_unit: clinician evaluations of model outputs (500 cardiac surgery cases x 4 models)

evidence.title: “Complex models, marginal benefits--a multi-centre development and validation study of early warning scores across 2·16 million patient admissions addressing intercurrent medical interventions”
evidence.outcome: Comparison of ML early warning model against NEWS and simpler scores on discrimination and net benefit
evidence.effect: XGB-EWS AUC 0.932 vs DEWS 0.908, NEWS 0.902, NEWS-Light 0.879; max net benefit difference 1.8 additional correct mortality identifications per 10,000 patients between XGB-EWS and NEWS.
evidence.quote: Decision curve analysis showed maximum net benefit differences of 1·8 additional correct mortality identifications per 10 000 patients between XGB-EWS and NEWS, and 1·7 per 10 000 between NEWS and NEWS-Light, across the evaluated risk thresholds.

evidence.title: Validation of several TB-CAD chest-X-ray applications in individuals with presumptive TB visiting peripheral health institutes in Delhi State
evidence.outcome: Head-to-head accuracy of seven TB-CAD products and radiologist on same data
evidence.effect: qXR performed as good as the radiologist; CAD4TB, Insight CXR, DrAid, Genki AUCROC adults ≥0.80, children ≥0.90; InferRead DR Chest and Radify Chest performed less well
evidence.quote: CAD4TB, Insight CXR, DrAid, and Genki also demonstrated high accuracy (AUCROC: adults ≥0.80, AUCROCs children ≥0.90), while InferRead DR Chest and Radify Chest performed less well.

evidence.title: Prompt Engineering Enables Open-Source LLMs to Match Proprietary Models in Diagnostic Accuracy for Annotation of Radiology Reports
evidence.outcome: Comparison of open-source Llama3 models against proprietary GPT-4o models on same annotation data
evidence.effect: GPT-4o highest accuracy 97.9%; Llama3.1-405b 97.1%, GPT-4o-mini 96.9%, Llama3-8b 96.9%, Llama3.1-70b 96.0%; open-source rivals proprietary
evidence.quote: Small, open-source LLMs can accurately annotate Danish trauma radiology reports when supported by effective prompt engineering, achieving accuracy levels that rival proprietary competitors.

evidence.title: Benchmarking Large Language Models and Clinicians Using Locally Generated Primary Healthcare Vignettes in Kenya
evidence.outcome: Blinded physician ratings of LLM versus clinician responses across 11 quality domains
evidence.effect: Clinician mean ratings were lower than LLMs in 9/11 domains, e.g. guideline alignment 2.86 vs 4.25-4.72; expert knowledge 2.76 vs 4.25-4.73; harm extent 3.16 vs 4.29-4.68.
evidence.quote: Clinician mean ratings were lower than those for LLMs in 9/11 domains: 2.86 vs 4.25-4.72 (guideline alignment), 2.76 vs 4.25-4.73 (expert knowledge), 2.96 vs 4.30-4.73 (logical coherence), and 2.58 vs 4.16-4.68 (low omission of critical information).

evidence.title: Comparative analysis of privacy-preserving open-source LLMs regarding extraction of diagnosticinformation from clinical CMR imaging reports
evidence.outcome: LLM diagnostic classification F1 versus board-certified cardiologist on same CMR reports
evidence.effect: Top four LLMs outperformed the cardiologist (F1 0.94) across all metrics; Gemma 2 achieved F1 0.98, Qwen2.5:32B 0.96, DeepseekR1-32B 0.95.
evidence.quote: The top four LLMs outperformed our board-certified cardiologist (F1 scoreof 0.94) across all evaluation metrics in analyzing CMR reports.

evidence.title: Development of an LLM Pipeline Surpassing Physicians in Cardiovascular Risk Score Calculation
evidence.outcome: Agreement with expert-adjudicated scores for pipeline vs standalone LLMs vs treating clinicians
evidence.effect: Mean Krippendorff's alpha 0.79 (pipeline) vs 0.32 (standalone LLMs) vs 0.31 (clinicians); Qwen3 pipeline had lower RMSE than clinicians for HAS-BLED (0.20 vs 0.87), CHA2DS2-VASc (0.53 vs 1.08), EuroSCORE II (1.99 vs 2.05).
evidence.quote: Pipeline-generated scores showed substantially higher agreement with expert adjudication than standalone LLMs and treating clinicians (mean Krippendorff’s alpha: 0.79 vs 0.32 vs 0.31) and demonstrated superior calibration.

evidence.title: Atlas-Assisted Bone Age Estimation from Hand–Wrist Radiographs Using Multimodal Large Language Models: A Comparative Study
evidence.outcome: Bone age error of four multimodal LLMs versus an experienced radiologist reference standard
evidence.effect: ChatGPT-5 MAE 1.46 years, ICC 0.849; Gemini 2.5 Pro MAE 2.24; Grok-3 MAE 3.14; Claude 4 Sonnet MAE 4.29 years. Only ChatGPT-5 deemed clinically useful.
evidence.quote: ChatGPT-5 demonstrated statistically superior performance with MAE of 1.46 years and ICC of 0.849, showing highest alignment with the reference standard.

evidence.title: Clinicians vs. Artificial Intelligence in Patient Outcome Prediction in the Intensive Care Unit
evidence.outcome: AI versus clinician predictions of ICU mortality, length of stay, delirium and AKI on the same patients
evidence.effect: Retrospectively AI generally outperformed single clinicians, but aggregated predictions from 7 clinicians outperformed AI. Prospectively subspecialized physicians generally outperformed AI, while trainees and nurses underperformed AI. Both were poor at length-of-stay prediction.
evidence.quote: In the prospective setting, subspecialized physicians generally outperformed AI, whereas physicians in training and nurses generally underperformed AI.

evidence.title: Blind Expert Evaluation of Open-Weight LLMs for Thyroid Cancer Patient Education in a Non-English Setting: GPT-OSS-20B vs MedGemma-27B-Instruct
evidence.outcome: Blinded endocrinologist ratings comparing two candidate LLMs on accuracy, completeness, clarity, utility, satisfaction
evidence.effect: GPT-OSS-20B rated higher than MedGemma-27B-Instruct on all five criteria after Holm correction; Satisfaction median 5.0 vs 4.0 (RBC 0.788), Completeness 5.0 vs 4.0 (RBC 0.599).
evidence.quote: GPT-OSS-20B achieved higher question-level median ratings than MedGemma-27B-Instruct across all five criteria after Holm correction.

evidence.title: Neurosymbolic Multi-Agent Artificial Intelligence versus General-Purpose Large Language Models for Clinical Decision Support in Ileus and Volvulus
evidence.outcome: Diagnostic accuracy of multi-agent system versus general-purpose LLMs on the same vignettes
evidence.effect: Multi-agent system 75.2% vs ChatGPT 60.2% and Gemini 58.6% (both p<0.001); hallucination 1.5% vs 15.0% and 9.8%; critical safety errors 0% vs 3.8% and 2.3%.
evidence.quote: The neurosymbolic multi-agent system achieved significantly higher diagnostic accuracy (75.2%; 95% CI: 66.9–82.2%) compared with ChatGPT (60.2%; 95% CI: 51.4–68.5%; p < 0.001) and Gemini (58.6%; 95% CI: 49.8–67.0%; p < 0.001).

evidence.title: Calibration Drift Under Cross-Institutional Deployment: An External Validation Framework for ICU Mortality Prediction Across MIMIC-IV and eICU
evidence.outcome: AUROC of XGBoost model versus APACHE score benchmark
evidence.effect: The model outperformed APACHE (AUROC 0.817 vs. 0.795; p < 0.001).
evidence.quote: The model outperformed APACHE (AUROC 0.817 vs. 0.795; p < 0.001).

evidence.title: CLINIKIOSK-An innovative technology to expand health care access
evidence.outcome: CliniKiosk RAG kiosk accuracy versus GPT-4o, Claude 3 Opus, Mixtral, Gemma on same cases
evidence.effect: Triage 88.6% for CliniKiosk; differential diagnosis >92% for all models (p=0.865); final diagnosis lower for CliniKiosk (76.0%); treatment accuracy 84.5%, GPT-4o and Claude Opus better (p<0.0001).
evidence.quote: Final-diagnosis accuracy was lower for CliniKiosk (76.0%) compared with other LLMs.

evidence.title: Large Language Model Performance in UK Advice & Guidance: A Pilot Study in Neurology
evidence.outcome: LLM compared with specialist neurologist responses on the same cases
evidence.effect: No significant differences across outcome, safety, efficacy, feasibility; unblinded raters preferred human responses across all domains; 10% of LLM responses concerning vs 0% human.
evidence.quote: Furthermore, unblinded results showed a preference for human responses, with human ratings being preferred across all domains.

evidence.title: Benchmarking General-Purpose and Medical AI Large Language Models for Clinical Assessment and Management in Parkinson’s Disease
evidence.outcome: Comparison of medically specialized LLM versus general-purpose LLM on appropriateness
evidence.effect: OpenEvidence vs Gemini: assessments 86.7% vs 80.0%, plans 57.8% vs 48.9%, both appropriate 55.6% vs 46.7%; no differences statistically significant.
evidence.quote: The medically specialized LLM demonstrated several qualitative advantages but no statistically significant performance benefit over the general-purpose model.

evidence.title: A Longitudinal Clinical Foundation Model on Nationwide Veteran Health Trajectories
evidence.outcome: 90-day mortality discrimination of new model versus operational CAN score on same patients
evidence.effect: VA-LLM AUROC 90.00% vs CAN 87.74% (p < 0.001); 45% relative AUPRC improvement; recalibrated Brier 0.0091 vs 0.0093
evidence.quote: VA-LLM achieved a 90-day mortality AUROC of 90.00% versus 87.74%

evidence.title: A real-world feasibility evaluation of LLM-based clinical prediction: emergency department return visit admission across two academic medical centers
evidence.outcome: LLM pipeline discrimination (AUC) versus traditional ML baselines for ED return visit admission at two sites
evidence.effect: At WCM Gemini ICL AUC 0.746 vs CatBoost 0.723 (DeLong p=0.044); at VUMC logistic regression AUC 0.799 matched GPT-5 mini 0.789 (n.s.).
evidence.quote: The LLM-based pipeline outperformed the strongest traditional ML baseline at WCM (Gemini ICL = 3 AUC 0.746 vs. CatBoost AUC 0.723; DeLong p = 0.044), but not at VUMC, where logistic regression on structured data alone (AUC 0.799) matched the best LLM configuration (GPT-5 mini AUC 0.789, n.s.).

evidence.title: Quality and Safety profiles of AI-Generated vs Clinician-Generated Handoffs in Hospital Medicine
evidence.outcome: Quality and safety ratings of AI handoffs versus clinician-authored handoffs
evidence.effect: Overall quality similar (3.7 vs 3.5, p=0.57); AI higher for completeness (4.1 vs 3.6) and organization (4.4 vs 4.1), lower for conciseness (3.7 vs 4.1) and accuracy (4.1 vs 4.4).
evidence.quote: Quality ratings were similar between AI and human handoffs (3.7 vs. 3.5, p=0.57).

evidence.title: Aligning Evaluation to Deployment: Measuring the Clinical Utility of End-to-End Deep Learning for Lung Cancer Screening
evidence.outcome: Cancer capture and net benefit of end-to-end models versus Lung-RADS and PLCOm2012 on same data
evidence.effect: Stronger end-to-end models had at least on-par or higher cancer capture and greater net benefit than Lung-RADS; on baseline scans capture exceeded Lung-RADS by more than 25 percentage points.
evidence.quote: On cumulative-gains curves and decision-curve analysis, the stronger end-to-end models achieved at least on-par or higher cancer capture and greater net benefit than Lung-RADS, and the advantage was largest on baseline scans, where Lung-RADS has no prior CT for comparison, exceeding it by more than 25 percentage points in capture.
evidence.sample_unit: LDCT scans (2,199 patients) from NLST test cohort

evidence.title: Comparison of the Visual Analysis Capabilities of Different Artificial Intelligence Models in Preoperative Patient Preparation Checks
evidence.outcome: Error detection accuracy of three competing AI models on the same simulated preoperative photographs
evidence.effect: Overall accuracy: ChatGPT 98.4%, Claude 84.0%, Copilot 73.6% (p < 0.001); surgical site marking verification: ChatGPT 98%, Claude 50%, Copilot 30%.
evidence.quote: Overall accuracy was highest with ChatGPT (98.4%), followed by Claude (84.0%) and Copilot (73.6%) (p < 0.001).

evidence.title: Multisite Real-World Validation of an Electronic Health Record-Integrated Generative Artificial Intelligence Tool for Venous Thromboembolism Risk Stratification
evidence.outcome: AI VTE risk classification sensitivity/specificity versus clinician order sets against physician-adjudicated reference standard
evidence.effect: iHGR 81.8% sensitivity, 70.9% specificity; checklist order set 61.3% sensitivity, 86.2% specificity; clinician judgement order set 78.1% sensitivity, 65.4% specificity.
evidence.quote: iHGR showed higher sensitivity for VTE risk than checklist-based order sets and clinician judgement without introducing systematic bias.

evidence.title: Agentic Artificial Intelligence for Hospital Readmission Review: A Single-Center Blinded Evaluation and Exploratory Qualitative Analysis
evidence.outcome: Blinded quality ratings of AI reviews versus physician reviews of the same readmissions
evidence.effect: Overall quality 4.35 (AI) vs 4.20 (physicians); mean difference 0.15, 95% CI -0.20 to 0.48; p=0.49; factuality and usefulness ratings also similar.
evidence.quote: Blinded overall quality ratings were similar for AI and physician reviews (4.35 vs. 4.20 on a 1-5 scale; mean difference 0.15, 95% CI -0.20 to 0.48; p=0.49), as were factuality/support and usefulness/actionability ratings.
evidence.sample_unit: readmissions (each reviewed by two physicians and the AI)

evidence.title: Expert-Rated Documentary Quality of AI-Assisted Hospital Discharge Reports: A Retrospective Paired Comparison with Physician-Written Reports
evidence.outcome: Expert-rated overall quality of AI-assisted vs physician-written discharge reports on the same cases
evidence.effect: IAIA achieved a higher overall mean rating than INF (8.14 vs. 7.30 out of 10; p < 0.0001; r ≈ 0.76); superior in 9 of 13 dimensions; non-blinded paired evaluation.
evidence.quote: IAIA achieved a significantly higher overall mean rating than INF (8.14 vs. 7.30 out of 10; p < 0.0001; r ≈ 0.76, large effect).
evidence.sample_unit: clinical cases (paired discharge reports; 240 reports total)

evidence.title: Development and External Validation of a Machine Learning Model for 10-Year Ischemic Stroke Risk Prediction in Diverse Populations
evidence.outcome: comparison with traditional risk scores
evidence.effect: M3 AUROC 0.813; ΔAUROC 0.164 vs rFSRP and 0.181 vs PCE; both P < 0.001.
evidence.quote: In the AoU test partition (n = 6,998; 384 cases), M3 achieved AUROC 0.813 (95% CI, 0.788–0.837), outperforming the Revised Framingham Stroke Risk Profile (ΔAUROC 0.164) and Pooled Cohort Equations (ΔAUROC 0.181; both  P < 0.001).
evidence.sample_unit: patients (34,987 All of Us development cohort; 10,693 BioMe external validation)

evidence.title: Patient-Facing AI Chatbots vs Primary Care Physicians: A Standardized Patient Field Experiment in China
evidence.outcome: Chatbot vs primary care physician diagnosis, medication, safety, and patient-centeredness on identical standardized patient cases
evidence.effect: Chatbots beat physicians on correct diagnosis (94.0% and 99.2% vs 30.6%) and patient-centeredness (3.28 and 3.35 vs 2.55). They had more unnecessary testing (90.3% and 96.4% vs 33.1%) and inappropriate medication (73.4% and 62.1% vs 23.4%).
evidence.quote: In this field experiment, patient-facing AI chatbots had higher diagnostic accuracy and patient-centered communication scores than PHC physicians, but were substantially more likely to recommend unnecessary tests and inappropriate medications.

evidence.title: Comparison of the Diagnostic Reliability of ChatGPT in Letournel–Judet Acetabulum Fracture Classification Based on Judet Radiographs According to Orthopaedic Residents
evidence.outcome: Comparison of AI classification performance against clinicians on same radiographs
evidence.effect: Both residents performed significantly better than ChatGPT-4o (p<0.001); residents' kappa 0.860 and 0.900 vs -0.014 for the AI.
evidence.quote: Both residents performed significantly better than the AI model (p< 0.001), with no significant difference observed between the residents (p= 0.070).

evidence.title: Standard-of-Care vs. Machine Learning–Recommended Discharge Destinations for Geriatric Surgical Inpatients: Algorithm Development and Internal Validation
evidence.outcome: Discharge destination accuracy of ML model versus standard-of-care decisions on same patients
evidence.effect: ML accuracy 82% (95% CI 0.76–0.86); 138 vs 124 correct versus standard of care, p = 0.041
evidence.quote: representing a significant improvement over standard-of-care decisions (138 vs 124 correct, p = 0.041)

evidence.title: SIGNAL: A Scalable, Real-World Model for Rapid Intraoperative Molecular Classification of Gliomas Using Stimulated Raman Histology
evidence.outcome: Comparison of candidate AI against prior model on the same data
evidence.effect: SIGNAL outperformed DeepGlioma on IDH mutation (93.51% vs. 79.22%), 1p19q codeletion (93.51% vs. 88.31%), and ATRX loss (89.61% vs. 83.98%).
evidence.quote: SIGNAL also outperformed DeepGlioma on all three molecular classification tasks, including IDH mutation (accuracy: 93.51% vs. 79.22%), 1p19q codeletion (93.51% vs. 88.31%), and ATRX loss (89.61% vs. 83.98%).

evidence.title: Uncertainty-Gated Glaucoma Screening: Combining Semi-Supervised Classification with Multi-Agent Large Language Model Deliberation
evidence.outcome: Accuracy of multi-agent VLM versus classifier on same flagged cases
evidence.effect: Agent system 89.5% accuracy (111/124) and 100% sensitivity versus classifier 73.4% (91/124); agents fixed 32 errors, introduced 12 new errors, net +20.
evidence.quote: On these flagged cases, the agent system achieves 100% sensitivity—detecting all 55 glaucoma cases with zero missed diagnoses—and 89.5% overall accuracy (111/124), compared to the classifier’s 73.4% (91/124).
evidence.sample_unit: held-out test patients (OCT; 124 flagged cases routed to agents)

evidence.title: Interpretable Machine Learning for Population-Level Severe Tooth Loss Prediction: A Two-Axis External Validation
evidence.outcome: EBM versus black-box ensemble AUC
evidence.effect: Zero-shot EBM AUC: 0.7591 versus black-box stacked meta-ensemble AUC: 0.7706.
evidence.quote: Notably, the zero-shot EBM (AUC: 0.7591) closely matched the predictive ceiling of a black-box stacked meta-ensemble (AUC: 0.7706), eliminating the need for unstable post-hoc approximations.
evidence.sample_unit: survey respondents (BRFSS 2022 derivation; also BRFSS 2024 N=448,213, NHANES 2015-2018 N=10,775)

evidence.title: Automated Extraction of Cancer Registry Data from Pathology Reports: Comparing LLM-Based and Ontology-Driven NLP Platforms
evidence.outcome: Extraction accuracy of LLM-based versus ontology-driven platform on same pathology reports
evidence.effect: Brim mean 96.7% pancreatic; T stage 96.4% vs DeepPhe 83.6% pancreatic and 70.6% breast; N stage comparable (96.4% pancreatic, 94.1% breast for DeepPhe).
evidence.quote: DeepPhe performed comparably for N stage (96.4% pancreatic, 94.1% breast) but had notable T stage deficits (83.6% pancreatic, 70.6% breast).

evidence.title: Cultryx: Precision Diagnostic Stewardship for Blood Cultures Using Machine Learning
evidence.outcome: Model AUROC/sensitivity versus SIRS, Shapiro Rule, physicians and GPT-5 for bacteremia prediction
evidence.effect: Cultryx outperformed all clinical heuristics (AUROC 0.810); SIRS specificity 41.2%; Shapiro sensitivity 70.2%; physicians with Fabre 95.7% sensitivity vs GPT-5 71.6%.
evidence.quote: In real-world benchmarking, Cultryx outperformed all clinical heuristics (AUROC 0.810).

evidence.title: Comparing computable structured phenotype- versus large language model-identification of opioid use disorder using electronic health record data
evidence.outcome: LLM vs structured phenotype diagnostic performance for OUD against physician chart review
evidence.effect: Structured phenotype sensitivity 0.84, specificity 0.964, PPV 0.58; LLM sensitivity 0.81, specificity 0.996, PPV 0.92; LLM specificity significantly higher (p<0.0001).
evidence.quote: Although the structured phenotype showed slightly higher sensitivity, the LLM achieved higher specificity and PPV, suggesting potential to reduce false-positive alerts in ED workflows.

evidence.title: Automated Task-Specific vs General-Purpose Artificial Intelligence for Detecting Subtle Intraoperative Warning Signs During Cataract Surgery: A Multicenter Diagnostic Study
evidence.outcome: F1 of AI models versus human graders at detecting anterior capsular radial folds
evidence.effect: Best general-purpose AI mean F1 0.519; fine-tuned max F1 0.606, inferior to humans. Automated task-specific model F1 0.869 (AUROC 0.958); top model 0.835 matched junior specialists (0.829), below seniors.
evidence.quote: In head-to-head comparison with clinicians, the top automated task-specific model (F1 score, 0.835) matched the performance of junior specialists (mean F1 score, 0.829) but remained below that of senior specialists.

evidence.title: A retrieval-augmented generation large language model framework for accurate dementia identification from electronic health records
evidence.outcome: Dementia identification F1, sensitivity, PPV for RAG LLM versus rule-based and keyword-filtered LLM on same labeled data
evidence.effect: RAG LLM F1=0.933, sensitivity 91.1%, PPV 95.5%; rule-based F1=0.823; keyword-filtered LLM F1=0.903, sensitivity 91.7%, PPV 88.6%.
evidence.quote: The RAG-based classifier achieved the highest performance (F1=0.933, sensitivity=91.1%, PPV=95.5%) compared to rule-based (F1=0.823, sensitivity=81.1%, PPV=83.5%) and keyword-filtered LLM (F1=0.903, sensitivity=91.7%, PPV=88.6%).

evidence.title: Cardiovascular risk scores for primary prevention: head-to-head validation of 16 established and contemporary models
evidence.outcome: Head-to-head comparison of 16 candidate risk models on the same cohort data
evidence.effect: Models differed markedly in calibration and net benefit; composite assessment favored PREVENT, QRISK2, PREDICT, PCE, and northern China-PAR variants.
evidence.quote: Composite assessment favored PREVENT, QRISK2, PREDICT, PCE, and northern China-PAR variants.

evidence.title: External Validation of Machine Learning Models for Traumatic Brain Injury: Performance, Efficiency, and Carbon Imprint
evidence.outcome: Comparing complex multiparameter ML models against simple pauci-parameter models on the same data: performance, net benefit, time, carbon
evidence.effect: Multiparameter models showed superior performance but not consistently better clinical utility; MULTI-PRE needed 100-fold longer inference and 10-fold higher carbon emissions with near-identical net benefit (0.06 vs 0.05).
evidence.quote: The best-performing multiparameter model (MULTI-PRE) required 100-fold longer inference time and 10-fold higher carbon emissions per prediction versus simple models, while net clinical benefit was nearly identical (0.06 vs 0.05).

evidence.title: Can a constrained AI clinical decision-support pipeline generate meal plans rated as highly as dietitian-designed plans? A blinded professional evaluation
evidence.outcome: Blinded dietitian ratings of AI-pipeline meal plans versus dietitian-designed plans
evidence.effect: AI plans scored 3.65 (SD 0.56) vs 3.12 (SD 0.73), d = 0.82; within-evaluator 31 vs 8 favored AI; paired t(39) = 4.72, P < 0.001; plan-level sign-test P = 0.06.
evidence.quote: AI-generated plans were rated at least as highly as dietitian-designed plans (within-evaluator, 31 vs 8 favored AI; paired t(39) = 4.72, P < 0.001) and higher in all 5 persona pairs, although the plan-level contrast was marginal (sign-test P = 0.06).

evidence.title: Safe Deployment of a Generative AI Assistant for Traditional-Medicine Education: Defense-in-Depth Architecture, Domain-Calibrated Safety Evaluation, and a Proposed Minimum Safety Stack
evidence.outcome: comparative safety versus commercial baselines
evidence.effect: TLAS-YHCT 100% safe-response rate versus 88.9% and 78.7% for two commercial baselines.
evidence.quote: A structured red-team of 206 attacks—constructed by domain-expert clinician-educators independent of system developers, scored blind by the same experts under a dual IT-security and clinical-education safety criterion—yielded a 100% safe-response rate versus 88.9% and 78.7% for two commercial baselines.

evidence.title: Assessing AI and Neurologist Diagnostic Reasoning Against Neuropathological Ground Truth
evidence.outcome: Top-3 and taxonomy-level diagnostic accuracy of AI versus neurologists on same cases against neuropathology
evidence.effect: DIAGNO matched or outperformed neurologists in top-3 accuracy (0.67 versus 0.63) and taxonomy-level accuracy (0.74 versus 0.66); more often correct in disagreements (29 versus 19 cases); also outperformed GPT-4o and DeepSeek R1.
evidence.quote: DIAGNO matched or outperformed neurologists in top-3 accuracy (0.67 versus 0.63) and taxonomy-level accuracy (0.74 versus 0.66).
evidence.sample_unit: retrospective case summaries with autopsy-confirmed diagnoses

evidence.title: A foundation-model-powered AI system with post-read alerts and concurrent assistance improves gastric biopsy diagnosis across 29 pathological categories
evidence.outcome: Foundation model versus conventional model performance
evidence.effect: Foundation model fine-tuned on 400 slides outperformed conventional model trained on over 10,000 slides.
evidence.quote: Furthermore, the foundation model fine-tuned on only 400 slides outperforms a conventional model trained on over 10,000 slides, demonstrating extreme data efficiency.
evidence.sample_unit: pathologists (reader study); 4,679 biopsies in retrospective multi-hospital simulation

evidence.title: General-Purpose vs. Domain-Specific Large Language Models in Antibiotic Clinical Decision-Making: A Double-Blind Evaluation with a 2×2 Factorial Design
evidence.outcome: Expert comprehensive scores of LLM antibiotic regimens versus real physician prescriptions on same cases
evidence.effect: Real physicians (4.76±0.04) > MedGo-CoT (4.58±0.09) > DeepSeek-CoT (4.41±0.11) > MedGo (4.25±0.16) > DeepSeek (3.98±0.20) (Friedman p<0.001).
evidence.quote: Score ranking: real physicians (4.76±0.04) > MedGo-CoT (4.58±0.09) > DeepSeek-CoT (4.41±0.11) > MedGo (4.25±0.16) > DeepSeek (3.98±0.20) (Friedman test, p<0.001).

evidence.title: Large-Scale Multi-Cancer Detection by Learning Segmentation from Reports
evidence.outcome: Tumor detection performance of R-Super versus radiologists and alternative AI models on same data
evidence.effect: R-Super significantly surpassed six radiologists in detecting six tumor types and matched them for uterus; detected 56% more malignant tumors at matched false positive rate; surpassed 6 alternative frameworks and 9 public AI models.
evidence.quote: R-Super significantly surpassed six radiologists in detecting six tumor types and matched them for uterus tumors in a reader study.
evidence.sample_unit: CT scans (internal UCSF N=2,301; external Stanford N=1,976, Medipol N=1,327, Basel N=2,935)

evidence.title: A framework for human-artificial intelligence co-learning for disease activity labeling using electronic health records
evidence.outcome: Accuracy and cost of budget-tiered configuration versus high-reasoning GPT-5.4 configuration
evidence.effect: Budget-tiered configuration matched GPT-5.4 high reasoning accuracy while reducing estimated cost by 69% and compute time by 70%.
evidence.quote: Applied across the cohort, the agent labeled 101,691 notes; the budget tiered configuration matched the accuracy of GPT-5.4 at high reasoning effort while reducing estimated cost by 69% and compute time by 70%.

evidence.title: Neuro-Symbolic AI for Automated Pathology Quality Measurement
evidence.outcome: Agreement with adjudicated gold standard, NSAI versus trained human abstractors, on same reports
evidence.effect: NSAI kappa 0.95 versus human abstractors kappa 0.92 against the same adjudicated gold standard; NSAI matched or modestly exceeded humans.
evidence.quote: The NSAI system's agreement with the adjudicated gold standard (Cohen's kappa = 0.95) matched or modestly exceeded that of the trained human abstractors measured against the same standard (kappa = 0.92), with particularly strong performance on Gastrointestinal Metaplasia (CAP 43).

evidence.title: Cyber-Physical Orchestration of Emergency Department Services Through a Bidirectional Digital Twin and a Deep Reinforcement Learning Agent: Architectural Design, In SilicoValidation, and Critical Analysis of Performance Under Demand Stress
evidence.outcome: DQN dispatch policy versus heuristic policies on peak occupancy and length of stay
evidence.effect: At +40% demand, DQN cut peak occupancy from 76.2 to 67.4 patients (-11.5%) with no length-of-stay penalty (98.31 vs 98.48 min; p = 0.878). At baseline load all policies were indistinguishable.
evidence.quote: Under baseline load, all four policies were statistically indistinguishable.
evidence.sample_unit: independent simulation seeds per configuration (four dispatch policies, four operating scenarios)

evidence.title: Cancer-Tissue Fraction as a Scanner-Robust Triage Signal for Automated Gleason Grading of Prostate Biopsies: External Validation Across a Middle Eastern Cohort
evidence.outcome: Deployed detect-then-grade pipeline agreement compared with ungated model and inter-pathologist ceiling
evidence.effect: Cross-validated all-slide QWK 0.86, 0.81, 0.86 across scanners, matching inter-pathologist ceiling of 0.81, versus 0.23 to 0.62 for the ungated model.
evidence.quote: At a 95% sensitivity operating point the deployed pipeline reached cross-validated all-slide QWK of 0.86, 0.81, and 0.86 (Grundium, Hamamatsu, Leica), matching the inter-pathologist ceiling of 0.81, against 0.23 to 0.62 for the ungated model.

evidence.title: Diagnostic Accuracy of a locally deployed Large Language Model Algorithm for Automated Code Stroke Pathway Identification in Emergency Department Triage Notes
evidence.outcome: Head-to-head accuracy comparison of six candidate LLMs on the same data
evidence.effect: Qwen 2.5 14B superior to Llama 3.1 8B, Phi-4 14B, Mistral 3 14B (all p<0.001 after Holm); no significant difference vs Nemotron-Nano-12B-v2 or Qwen 3 14B.
evidence.quote: Pairwise McNemar testing demonstrated statistically superior overall accuracy for Qwen 2.5 14B over Llama 3.1 8B, Phi-4 14B, and Mistral 3 14B (all p<0.001 after Holm correction), with no significant difference detected versus Nemotron-Nano-12B-v2 or Qwen 3 14B.

evidence.title: ChatGPT-4 Based Automated Preliminary Clinical Reporting in Myocardial Perfusion Imaging: A Pilot Evaluation
evidence.outcome: Clinical accuracy of ChatGPT-4 reports versus physician reports on Likert scale
evidence.effect: ChatGPT-4 scored lower than physicians on clinical accuracy, especially in complex cases (p = 0.002, exploratory, n=30); strong on structure, terminology, comprehensibility.
evidence.quote: Statistical analysis indicated a significant difference in clinical accuracy compared to physician reports (p = 0.002, exploratory analysis, n=30).

evidence.title: Harnessing Pathology Foundation Models to Accelerate Lymphoma Diagnosis Through Automated Immunohistochemistry Triage
evidence.outcome: AI subtype prediction accuracy compared with practicing pathologists on the same cases
evidence.effect: HATS 85% versus pathologists 65% accuracy for predicting lymphoma subtypes from morphology alone.
evidence.quote: In a blinded reader study, HATS outperforms practicing pathologists at predicting lymphoma subtypes from morphology alone (85% vs 65%).

evidence.title: Machine learning for elective caesarean section in Bangladesh: validation design, not model choice, determines the performance a deployed model would have
evidence.outcome: Comparison of complex ML models against logistic regression baseline
evidence.effect: No model improved on logistic regression by a margin worth acting on; AUC ranged 0.724 to 0.736 under cluster-grouped validation, spread 0.012.
evidence.quote: No model improved on logistic regression by a margin worth acting on: the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve ranged from 0.724 to 0.736 under cluster-grouped validation, a spread of 0.012.

evidence.title: Antimicrobial Stewardship in the Era of AI: A Head-to-Head Comparison of a Machine Learning HTL Algorithm and Large Language Models in Real-World Infectious Disease Cases
evidence.outcome: Agreement of antimicrobial recommendations with expert consensus, compared across a specialized ML tool and general LLMs
evidence.quote: The ML-HTL system showed the highest agreement with the expert´s consensus (90.9%; 95% CI: 83.1–95.3), followed by GPT-4 (63.6%; 95% CI: 53.2–72.9) and Gemini (37.5%; 95% CI: 28.1–47.9).

evidence.title: Automating the triage of rheumatology outpatient referrals: a comparative evaluation of 23 large language models under simple and advanced prompting
evidence.outcome: LLM triage accuracy versus expert consensus and published human triage accuracy
evidence.effect: Leading models matched expert consensus on most cases, within or above the range reported for human triage; LLMs categorise urgency as well or better than published human triage systems.
evidence.quote: Leading models matched expert consensus on most cases, within or above the range reported for human triage.
evidence.sample_unit: referral scenarios (each triaged 3 times by 23 LLMs under 2 prompt conditions)

evidence.title: Explainable Machine Learning and Temporal Calibration Drift of a TyG- BMI-Based Model for Early Prediction of Gestational Diabetes Mellitus
evidence.outcome: comparative temporal AUC
evidence.effect: Temporal validation AUCs: XGBoost 0.881 (95% CI 0.819–0.933), LightGBM 0.870, logistic regression 0.857.
evidence.quote: In temporal validation, XGBoost showed the highest discrimination (AUC 0.881, 95% CI 0.819–0.933), followed by LightGBM (0.870) and logistic regression (0.857).

evidence.title: Adaptive forecasting of antiretroviral therapy demand using machine learning in India’s national HIV programme
evidence.outcome: Signed percentage deviation of foundation/hybrid models versus classical baselines across ART regimens
evidence.effect: No single model best across regimens. Hybrid 70th percentile SPD -2.02% for adult AZT+3TC vs other models' range [-15.7, 8.87]; Holt-Winters best for adult RTV booster (1.68% vs 14.94-17.25%).
evidence.quote: Performance varied across regimens, indicating that no single approach was best-performing for all formulations.
evidence.sample_unit: regimen-specific monthly national ART consumption time series

evidence.title: Evaluating General-Purpose versus Medical-Specific Large Language Models for Perioperative Deep Vein Thrombosis Consultation: Perspectives from Physicians, Nurses, and Patients
evidence.outcome: Quality, empathy and readability of responses from competing general-purpose vs medical-specific LLMs on the same questions
evidence.effect: General-purpose models scored higher than medical-specific models across all outcomes; in patients QAMAI 26.0 vs 21.2 (P=0.001), GQS 4.0 vs 2.6 (P=0.007), PETS 75.2 vs 57.6 (P=0.005).
evidence.quote: General-purpose models consistently scored higher than medical-specific models across all outcomes and evaluator groups.
evidence.sample_unit: evaluators (5 physicians, 5 nurses, 5 patients) rating responses to 9 questions from 4 LLMs

evidence.title: Half of alcohol, drug, and self-harm presentations cannot be identified in coded emergency department data: a diagnostic accuracy study of a large language model
evidence.outcome: LLM balanced accuracy versus clinician review and clinical coding for alcohol, drug, self-harm identification
evidence.effect: LLM balanced accuracy matched or outperformed clinician review (alcohol 0.942 v 0.930, p=0.635; drug 0.959 v 0.791, p<0.001; self-harm 0.982 v 0.908, p=0.004); coding identified 6.0% vs reference 12.1%.
evidence.quote: LLM balanced accuracy matched or outperformed clinician review in all three domains (alcohol 0.942 v 0.930, p=0.635; drug 0.959 v 0.791, p<0.001; self-harm 0.982 v 0.908, p=0.004).
evidence.sample_unit: emergency department attendances (validation week); 105,096 annual attendances

evidence.title: Disease Spectrum Analysis and AI-Assisted Screening of Fundus Disorders Using Portable Handheld Fundus Imaging in Health Examination Populations
evidence.outcome: Comparative performance of lightweight networks versus retinal foundation models on handheld fundus data
evidence.effect: Lightweight models achieved favorable performance; retinal foundation models pre-trained on conventional fundus data showed limited advantages. Screening AUC 0.9612; fine-grained classification macro-AUC 0.8445.
evidence.quote: Retinal foundation models, pre‑trained on conventional adult fundus datasets, showed limited performance advantages in this portable imaging scenario.

evidence.title: Are Frontier Large Language Models Safer Than Government-Backed Symptom Checkers for Clinical Self-Triage? A Standardised Vignette Evaluation
evidence.outcome: Triage accuracy of LLMs versus existing government symptom checker on same vignettes
evidence.effect: Healthdirect 48.9% accuracy (kappa 0.233) versus 73.3% to 86.7% for LLMs (kappa 0.600 to 0.800); Cochran's Q = 36.79, p < 0.001.
evidence.quote: Healthdirect achieved 48.9% accuracy (95% CI 35.0% to 63.0%; kappa = 0.233) versus 73.3% to 86.7% for LLMs (kappa = 0.600 to 0.800).

evidence.title: From National Data to Local Evaluation: Benchmarking Machine Learning Models for Perioperative Risk Prediction
evidence.outcome: AUROC of complex ML models versus logistic regression and NSQIP Surgical Risk Calculator on identical cases
evidence.effect: FT-Transformer exceeded logistic regression by only 0.009–0.030 AUROC; calculator matched best model for mortality but trailed for any complication.
evidence.quote: The FT-Transformer led or tied on AUROC for all four outcomes (0.755–0.955), exceeding logistic regression by only 0.009–0.030; the three encoders fell 0.005–0.009 short of the best tabular model and spanned 0.003 or less.
evidence.sample_unit: surgical cases (temporal test set, 2024 ACS NSQIP)

evidence.title: Performance, safety, and repeated-query stability of large language models versus early-career urologists in urological oncology: a source-masked vignette benchmark
evidence.outcome: Composite success of LLMs versus early-career urologists on the same vignettes
evidence.effect: Primary composite success was 70%, 64%, 60% for LLMs versus 85% and 89% for urologists (Cochran's Q = 34.23; P < 0.001); safety-critical errors 25-26% vs 1-2%.
evidence.quote: Primary composite success was achieved in 70/100 (70.0%) GPT-5.2, 64/100 (64.0%) Claude, and 60/100 (60.0%) Gemini responses, versus 85/100 (85.0%) and 89/100 (89.0%) for Urologists A and B (Cochran’s Q = 34.23; P < 0.001).

evidence.title: MDT-guided language-model reasoning for spinal infection diagnosis
evidence.outcome: balanced accuracy versus zero-shot baseline
evidence.effect: Infection identification improved by 3.63 and 1.48 points; tuberculous-aetiology differences were -5.48 and − 5.40 points.
evidence.quote: Structured MDT-guided reasoning consistently improved broad infection recognition across models and centres, whereas its benefit did not extend to tuberculous-aetiology differentiation.

evidence.title: A Treatment-Trajectory Framework for Deployment- Oriented Prediction of Acute Care Utilization in Oncology
evidence.outcome: AUROC versus conventional patient-level model
evidence.effect: Trajectory-aware AUROC 0.831 vs. conventional 0.785.
evidence.quote: The trajectory-aware model achieved higher discrimination (AUROC, 0.831 vs. 0.785) with the global top 5% risk stratum captured 19.0% of ACU events with 68.1% positive predictive value.

evidence.title: Generative Artificial Intelligence for Opportunistic Osteoporosis Screening Using Lumbar Spine Imaging: Diagnostic Performance, Reproducibility, Effects of Few-Shot Prompting, and Comparison with Physicians
evidence.outcome: Diagnostic accuracy of generative AI vs specialists and non-specialists at -1.0 cutoff on radiographs
evidence.effect: Claude 73.3%, Gemini 64.4%, specialists 57.4%, ChatGPT 55.6%, non-specialists 44.0%; performance model-dependent.
evidence.quote: Claude achieved the highest radiographic accuracy (73.3%), followed by Gemini (64.4%), specialists (57.4%), ChatGPT (55.6%), and non-specialists (44.0%).
evidence.sample_unit: images (45 lateral lumbar radiographs and 45 sagittal CT images)

evidence.title: The Diagnostic and Triage Accuracy of the GPT-3 Artificial Intelligence Model
evidence.outcome: GPT-3 diagnostic and triage accuracy compared with physicians and lay adults on the same vignettes
evidence.effect: Top-3 diagnosis: GPT-3 88% vs lay 54% (p<0.001) and physicians 96% (p=0.0354). Triage: GPT-3 71% vs lay 74% (p=0.73) and physicians 91% (p<0.001).
evidence.quote: Among all cases, GPT-3 replied with the correct diagnosis in its top 3 for 88% (95% CI, 75% to 94%) of cases, compared to 54% (95% CI, 53% to 55%) for lay individuals (p<0.001) and 96% (95% CI, 94% to 97%) for physicians (p=0.0354).

evidence.title: Exploration of ChatGPT application in diabetes education: a multi-dataset, multi-reviewer study
evidence.outcome: Helpfulness and trustworthiness versus physicians
evidence.effect: ChatGPT lower than physicians: helpfulness 4.18 vs. 4.91, P <0.001; trustworthiness 4.80 vs. 5.20, P = 0.042.
evidence.quote: In the real-world dataset evaluation, ChatGPT responses received lower ratings compared to physicians’ responses (helpfulness: 4.18 vs. 4.91, P <0.001; trustworthiness: 4.80 vs. 5.20, P = 0.042).

evidence.title: Evaluating the use of GPT-3.5-turbo to provide clinical recommendations in the Emergency Department
evidence.outcome: Accuracy of GPT-3.5-turbo recommendations compared with a resident physician on the same ED visits
evidence.effect: GPT-3.5-turbo performed poorly compared to a resident physician, with accuracy scores 24% lower on average.
evidence.quote: We find that GPT-3.5-turbo performs poorly compared to a resident physician, with accuracy scores 24% lower on average.

evidence.title: AI facilitated sperm detection in azoospermic samples for use in ICSI
evidence.outcome: AI versus embryologist speed and accuracy identifying sperm in still images on same data
evidence.effect: AI was faster (0.019±0.30 x 10-5 s vs 36.10±1.18s per field, P<0.0001) and more accurate (91.95±0.81% vs 86.52±1.34%, P<0.001); AI found 611 of 688 sperm vs 560 by embryologist.
evidence.quote: In cohort 1, the AI model showed improvement in time-taken to identify all sperm per field of view (0.019±0.30 x 10 -5 s versus 36.10±1.18s, P<0.0001) and improved accuracy (91.95±0.81% vs 86.52±1.34%, P<0.001) compared to an embryologist.

evidence.title: GPT-4 and Neurologists in Screening for Mild Cognitive Impairment in the Elderly: A Comparative Analysis Study
evidence.outcome: MCI screening accuracy of GPT-4 versus three junior neurologists on same participant corpus
evidence.effect: GPT-4 accuracy 0.81 versus neurologists 0.41 to 0.49; GPT-4 discriminated MCI better, p < 0.001
evidence.quote: Results showed that the GPT-4 model had higher accuracy (0.81) compared to the neurologists (ranging from 0.41 to 0.49).

evidence.title: Clinical implementation and evaluation of deep learning-assisted automatic radiotherapy treatment planning for lung cancer
evidence.outcome: Overall plan quality (PQM) of DL-assisted automatic plans versus manual clinical plans on the same patients
evidence.effect: PQM 40.7 ± 13.1 manual vs 40.8 ± 13.5 automatic, equivalent quality; planning time 103.1 to 32.6 min (P<0.001); MUs 789.9 to 692.5 (P<0.001).
evidence.quote: The average PQM score was 40.7 ± 13.1 for manual plans and 40.8 ± 13.5 for automatic plans, and they had equivalent overall plan quality.

evidence.title: Retrieval Augmented Generation Enabled Generative Pre-Trained Transformer 4 (GPT-4) Performance for Clinical Trial Screening
evidence.outcome: Accuracy, sensitivity, specificity of RECTIFIER versus study staff screening against expert clinician gold standard
evidence.effect: Eligibility sensitivity/specificity 92.3%/93.9% for RECTIFIER vs 90.1%/83.6% for study staff; symptomatic heart failure accuracy 97.9% vs 91.7%, MCC 0.924 vs 0.721.
evidence.quote: RECTIFIER performed better than study staff to determine the inclusion criteria of “symptomatic heart failure” with an accuracy of 97.9% vs 91.7% and an MCC of 0.924 vs 0.721, respectively.

evidence.title: Consensus, dissensus and synergy between clinicians and specialist foundation models in radiology report generation
evidence.outcome: Radiologist panel preference for AI reports versus clinician-written reports
evidence.effect: 55.4% of ICU AI reports were preferable or equivalent to clinician reports by half or more of the panel, 77.7% for outpatient X-rays overall, and 94% for cases with no pertinent abnormal findings.
evidence.quote: We observe a wide distribution of preferences across the panel, ranging from full consensus to dissensus, across clinical settings and regions, with 55.4% of Flamingo-CXR intensive care reports evaluated to be preferable or equivalent to clinician reports, by half or more of the panel, rising to 77.7% for outpatient x-rays overall and to 94% for the subset of cases with no pertinent abnormal findings.
evidence.sample_unit: certified radiologists evaluating AI-generated and human-written chest radiograph reports

evidence.title: Artificial intelligence to facilitate clinical trial recruitment in age-related macular degeneration
evidence.outcome: PPV and number of eligible GA trial patients shortlisted, AI vs keyword EHR search
evidence.effect: AI shortlisted 1,139 patients (PPV 63%; 95% CI 54–71%) vs EHR search 693 (PPV 40%; 95% CI 39–42%). Combined AI-EHR: 604 patients, PPV 86%.
evidence.quote: The AI system shortlisted a larger number of eligible patients with greater precision (1,139, PPV: 63%; 95% CI: 54–71%) compared to the EHR search (693, PPV: 40%; 95% CI: 39– 42%).

evidence.title: The Transformative Potential of Large Language Models in Mining Electronic Health Records Data
evidence.outcome: LLM accuracy compared with physicians on the same comorbidity extraction reports
evidence.effect: GPT-4 outperformed physicians (McNemar p<0.001); sensitivity 96.8% vs 88.8% for physicians; physicians slightly better in precision (97.7% vs 96.8%). GPT-3.5 not significantly different (p=0.79).
evidence.quote: GPT-4 demonstrated clear superiority in several key metrics (McNemar’s test p < 0.001).

evidence.title: Using Large Language Models to Annotate Complex Cases of Social Determinants of Health in Longitudinal Clinical Records
evidence.outcome: Comparison of GPT-4 against GPT-3.5, NER model, RegEx and human annotators on same notes
evidence.effect: GPT-4 had the highest performance among automated methods and higher recall than humans (0.924 vs 0.702) but lower precision (0.850 vs 0.971).
evidence.quote: Compared with GPT-3.5 and the NER model, GPT-4 had the highest performance and had a much higher recall (0.924) than human annotators (0.702) in identifying patients experiencing current or past housing instability, although precision was lower (0.850) compared with human annotators (0.971).

evidence.title: Evaluating the Effectiveness and Safety of Large Language Model in Generating Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus Management Plans: A Comparative Study with Medical Experts Based on Real Patient Records
evidence.outcome: Error scores of GPT-4 versus blinded medical experts on the same patient records
evidence.effect: Overall error scores were comparable between experts and GPT-4 (p=0.301). Experts had fewer missing medications (p=0.008), and GPT-4 had fewer unnecessary medications (p=0.003).
evidence.quote: The overall error scores were comparable between human experts and GPT-4 (p=0.301).

evidence.title: Performance of a Protein Language Model for Variant Annotation in Cardiac Disease
evidence.outcome: VUS reclassification rate of candidate AI versus another variant classification platform on same variants
evidence.effect: Reclassification rate was 86.1% for VarCard.io vs 34.8% for Franklin (p<0.001), showing large differences between competing tools on the same data.
evidence.quote: The reclassification rate was significantly higher for VarCard.io than for Franklin (86.1% vs 34.8%, p<0.001).

evidence.title: Customizing GPT-4 for clinical information retrieval from standard operating procedures
evidence.outcome: Sufficient answers from GPT-4 versus Claude-3-opus on the same questions
evidence.effect: Claude-3-opus outperformed GPT-4 in providing sufficient answers (70.0% vs. 36.7%) and required fewer iterations for satisfactory responses.
evidence.quote: Comparing LLMs, Claude-3-opus outperformed GPT-4 in providing sufficient answers (70.0% vs. 36.7%) and required fewer iterations for satisfactory responses.

evidence.title: Large language models for accurate disease detection in electronic health records
evidence.outcome: LLM versus regex method accuracy for gout detection against gold standard on same paragraphs
evidence.effect: LLM outperformed regex, achieving 92.7% PPV, 96.6% NPV, and 95.4% accuracy for gout.
evidence.quote: The LLM-based algorithm outperformed the regex method, achieving a 92.7% [88.7-95.4%] positive predictive value, a 96.6% [94.6-97.8%] negative predictive value, and an accuracy of 95.4% [93.6-96.7%] for gout.

evidence.title: Predicting onward care needs at admission to reduce discharge delay using machine learning
evidence.outcome: ML prediction of discharge care needs compared against clinician predictions and a hybrid model
evidence.effect: ML performance comparable to clinician predictions despite using a subset of information; each performs better for different care need types; hybrid clinician+ML model more accurate.
evidence.quote: The model performance is comparable to clinician’s predictions of discharge care needs, despite working with only a subset of the information available to the clinician.

evidence.title: Evaluating the accuracy and reliability of large language models in assisting with pediatric differential diagnoses: A multicenter diagnostic study
evidence.outcome: Fine-tuned GPT-3 differential diagnosis accuracy compared with human physicians on same test set
evidence.effect: Model accuracy 87% (131/150) vs physicians 91%; P = .47, comparable performance; sensitivity 85%, specificity 90%, precision 88%, F1 0.87.
evidence.quote: The model’s performance was comparable to human physicians (accuracy 91%; P = .47).

evidence.title: Real-World Performance of Large Language Models in Emergency Department Chest Pain Triage and the development of MediGuide-14B
evidence.outcome: Diagnostic accuracy and specificity for ACS in chest pain triage, LLMs versus human experts
evidence.effect: MediGuide-14B accuracy 87.52% and specificity 78.63%, versus human experts 86.37% accuracy and 89.26% specificity. Accuracy was comparable, but specificity was lower than the experts'.
evidence.quote: MediGuide-14B demonstrated the highest accuracy (87.52%) and specificity (78.63%), comparable to human experts (86.37% accuracy, 89.26% specificity).

evidence.title: Expert-Level Detection of Referable Glaucoma from Fundus Photographs in a Safety Net Population: The AI and Teleophthalmology in Los Angeles Initiative
evidence.outcome: Algorithm AUC/sensitivity/specificity compared with clinician graders on same test set
evidence.effect: Algorithm matched or exceeded all independent clinician graders (AUC 0.92 vs optometrist labels, 0.93 vs expert panel labels); grader sensitivity 0.33-0.99, specificity 0.68-0.98.
evidence.quote: Algorithm performance matched or exceeded that of all independent clinician graders in detecting patient-level referable glaucoma based on LAC DHS optometrist (AUC = 0.92) or expert panel (AUC = 0.93) reference labels.

evidence.title: Large Language Model Augmented Clinical Trial Screening
evidence.outcome: Comparison of GPT-3.5 vs GPT-4 and prompting approaches on the same data
evidence.effect: GPT-4 median criterion accuracy 0.838 vs GPT-3.5 0.761; GPT-4 generally outperformed GPT-3.5 but at higher cost ($0.15–$0.27 vs $0.02–$0.03) and time (7.9–12.4 vs 1.4–3 min).
evidence.quote: LLM performance varies by prompt, with GPT-4 generally outperforming GPT-3.5, but at higher costs and longer processing times.

evidence.title: Ubie Symptom Checker: A Clinical Vignette Simulation Study
evidence.outcome: Symptom checker Top-5 hit accuracy compared with physicians and comparator symptom checkers on same vignettes
evidence.effect: Ubie Top-5 hit accuracy 63.4%, Top-10 71.6%; compared favorably to the median physician hit accuracy and comparator symptom checkers.
evidence.quote: When compared to physicians and comparator SC’s that used the same clinical vignettes set, Ubie compared favorably to the median physician hit accuracy.

evidence.title: Physician- and Large Language Model-Generated Hospital Discharge Summaries: A Blinded, Comparative Quality and Safety Study
evidence.outcome: Blinded reviewer quality and preference for LLM versus physician discharge summary narratives
evidence.effect: Overall quality 3.67 vs 3.77 (p=0.213); preference p=0.270; LLM more concise and coherent but less comprehensive, with more errors (2.91 vs 1.82 per summary).
evidence.quote: Across 100 encounters, LLM- and physician-generated narratives were comparable in overall quality on a 1-5 Likert scale (average 3.67 [SD 0.49] vs 3.77 [SD 0.57], p=0.213) and reviewer preference (χ2 = 5.2, p=0.270).
evidence.sample_unit: inpatient hospital medicine encounters (discharge summary narratives)

evidence.title: Real-World Evaluation of Artificial Intelligence (AI) Chatbots for Providing Sexual Health Information: A Consensus Study Using Clinical Queries
evidence.outcome: Chatbot performance compared with nurse responses on the same sexual health questions
evidence.effect: Chatbots compared with human clinicians (nurses) by blinded expert panel; chatbots showed potential as adjuncts but all were susceptible to generating incorrect information.
evidence.quote: However, all AI chatbots showed susceptibility to generating incorrect information.

evidence.title: Is it time for the neurologist to use Large Language Models in everyday practice?
evidence.outcome: Diagnostic accuracy of LLMs versus neurologists on same real-world cases
evidence.effect: Neurologists achieved 75% diagnostic accuracy, outperforming ChatGPT-3.5 (54%) and Gemini (46%).
evidence.quote: Neurologists achieved a diagnostic accuracy of 75%, outperforming ChatGPT-3.5 (54%) and Gemini (46%).

evidence.title: Hazard-aware adaptations bridge the generalization gap in large language models: a nationwide study
evidence.outcome: Lung cancer screening eligibility identification
evidence.effect: Adapted LLM identified eligibility in 59% versus 8% with current national VA tools.
evidence.quote: As a potential clinical application, our adapted LLM system identified lung cancer screening eligibility in 59% of Veterans who later developed the disease, compared to 8% with current national VA tools.
evidence.sample_unit: notes and LLM outputs analyzed for error codification

evidence.title: Unmet Needs in Acute Hepatic Porphyria Diagnosis: A Comparative Big Data Analysis of an AI-based Human-in-the-Loop Screening Versus Standard of Care
evidence.outcome: Rate of clinically plausible AHP cases (precision) in AI human-in-the-loop screening versus standard of care
evidence.effect: 74 (38.74%) of 191 HAI cases vs 28 (27.72%) of 107 SOC cases were clinically plausible; 46 de-novo cases missed by SOC; difference not statistically significant.
evidence.quote: In our study, our proposed HAI screening approach showed a higher plausibility rate in suspected cases compared to the SOC and statistical testing could not find a statistically significant difference between the screening methods.

evidence.title: A Comparative Study of Predictive model (ECG Buddy) and ChatGPT-4o for Myocardial Infarction Diagnosis via ECG image Analysis: Performance, Accuracy, and Clinical Feasibility
evidence.outcome: Diagnostic performance of specialized ECG AI versus general LLM on same ECG dataset for MI classification
evidence.effect: ECG Buddy accuracy 96.98% vs ChatGPT 65.95%; AUC 98.8% vs 57.34%; sensitivity 96.65% vs 36.40%; DeLong's test P < .001.
evidence.quote: DeLong’s test confirmed that ECG Buddy significantly outperformed ChatGPT (all P < .001).

evidence.title: An interpretable model predicts visual outcomes of no light perception eyes after open globe injury
evidence.outcome: AUC of ML model versus ophthalmologists and Ocular Trauma Score on same cases
evidence.effect: VisionGo AUC 0.75 and 0.90 vs OTS 0.49; vs ophthalmologists 0.73 vs 0.57 (previtrectomy) and 0.87 vs 0.64 (intravitrectomy)
evidence.quote: VisionGo showed better performance than ophthalmologists in both previtrectomy and intravitrectomy application scenarios (AUC=0.73 vs 0.57 and 0.87 vs 0.64).

evidence.title: PI-RADSAI: introducing a new human-in-the-loop AI model for prostate cancer diagnosis based on MRI
evidence.outcome: AI diagnostic AUC for clinically significant PCa versus 11 general radiologists on same data
evidence.effect: PI-RADS-AI outperformed 5/11 (45.5%) and matched 3/11 (27.3%) general radiologists; AUC internal 0.801 vs 0.770, p<0.01; external 0.833 vs 0.867, p=0.309.
evidence.quote: In the paired test, PI-RADS<sup>AI</sup> outperformed 5/11 (45.5%) and matched the performance of 3/11 (27.3%) general radiologists in achieving a clinically significant PCa diagnosis (area under the curve, internal test, 0.801 vs. 0.770, p < 0.01; external test, 0.833 vs. 0.867, p = 0.309).
evidence.sample_unit: biopsy-naïve patients (MRI data from four centres)

evidence.title: Evaluation of a convolution neural network for baseline total tumor metabolic volume on [18F]FDG PET in diffuse large B cell lymphoma
evidence.outcome: agreement with semi-automated reference
evidence.effect: AI+review method 3 vs reference method 5: ICC 0.99 for TMTV and 1.0 for TLG.
evidence.quote: Between methods 3 and 5, for the main user, the ICC was 0.99 for TMTV and 1.0 for TLG.

evidence.title: Validation in Indonesia of two published scores for mortality prediction after cardiac surgery
evidence.outcome: model discrimination comparison
evidence.effect: EuroSCORE II AUC 0.774 (0.714–0.834) versus ACEF AUC 0.638 (0.561–0.718); AUC difference P = 0.007.
evidence.quote: The EuroSCORE II had good discrimination with AUC 0.774 (0.714–0.834), whereas the ACEF score had poor discrimination with AUC 0.638 (0.561–0.718).

evidence.title: Identification of Active Pulmonary Tuberculosis Among Patients With Positive Interferon-Gamma Release Assay Results: Value of a Deep Learning-based Computer-aided Detection System in Different Scenarios of Implementation
evidence.outcome: CAD sensitivity versus radiologists on the same data in reader test
evidence.effect: CAD sensitivity 72.7% vs. radiologists 59.5% (P=0.005) at the same specificity of 88.0%.
evidence.quote: In the reader test, the CAD exhibited a higher sensitivity than radiologists (72.7% vs. 59.5%; P =0.005) at the same specificity (88.0%), and CAD-assisted interpretation significantly improved the sensitivity of radiologists' interpretation (72.3%; P <0.001).

evidence.title: External Validation and Comparison of a General Ward Deterioration Index Between Diversely Different Health Systems
evidence.outcome: Comparison of PICTURE against Epic Deterioration Index and NEWS on the same data
evidence.effect: PICTURE outperformed both the Epic Deterioration Index and the National Early Warning Score at both institutions.
evidence.quote: PICTURE also outperformed both the Epic Deterioration Index and the National Early Warning Score at both institutions.

evidence.title: Recalibration of a Deep Learning Model for Low-Dose Computed Tomographic Images to Inform Lung Cancer Screening Intervals
evidence.outcome: AUC for predicting 1-year lung cancer risk, deep learning vs statistical model vs Lung-RADS on same data
evidence.effect: Recalibrated LCP-CNN AUC 0.87 vs LCRAT + CT 0.79 and Lung-RADS 0.69 (P < .001); lower 1-year delay risk at 66% biennial assignment (0.28% vs 0.60% vs 0.97%).
evidence.quote: The recalibrated LCP-CNN had substantially higher area under the curve (0.87) than LCRAT + CT (0.79) or Lung-RADS (0.69) to predict 1-year lung cancer risk (P < .001).
evidence.sample_unit: LDCT images (screens with presumed nonmalignant nodules)

evidence.title: How smart is artificial intelligence in organs delineation? Testing a CE and FDA-approved Deep-Learning tool using multiple expert contours delineated on planning CT images
evidence.outcome: Comparison of DL auto-contours and DL-assisted contours versus manual expert contours on same CT data
evidence.effect: DSC of adjusted MV contours statistically significantly higher than manual ones overall; median DSC 0.99/0.98 versus 0.83/0.81 by slice thickness.
evidence.quote: Overall, the DSC values obtained in the MD&MV subgroup were statistically significantly higher than MD one.

evidence.title: Prognostic Value of Machine-Learning-Based PRAISE Score for Ischemic and Bleeding Events in Patients With Acute Coronary Syndrome Undergoing Percutaneous Coronary Intervention
evidence.venue: Journal of the American Heart Association
evidence.outcome: PRAISE compared with GRACE 2.0, PRECISE-DAPT, and PARIS on discrimination, calibration, reclassification, net benefit
evidence.effect: PRAISE displayed slightly greater net benefit than GRACE for 1-year death risk at 5%-10% threshold; overall performance limited.
evidence.quote: Based on the decision curve analysis, the PRAISE score displayed a slightly greater net benefit for the 1-year risk of death (5%-10%) than the GRACE score did.

evidence.title: Collaborative strategies for deploying artificial intelligence to complement physician diagnoses of acute respiratory distress syndrome
evidence.outcome: AI model accuracy compared with physicians on the same chest X-rays
evidence.effect: AI accuracy 0.847 (0.806–0.887) vs physicians 0.808 (0.767–0.85), p<0.05; sensitivity 0.789 vs 0.727.
evidence.quote: Overall, the deep learning-based AI system had significantly higher accuracy in detecting ARDS images compared to physicians (0.847 [95% CI 0.806–0.887] vs. 0.808 [95% CI 0.767–0.85], p value of < 0.05 using the one-sided bootstrapped two-sample hypothesis testing) (Table 2 ).

evidence.title: Explainable artificial intelligence incorporated with domain knowledge diagnosing early gastric neoplasms under white light endoscopy
evidence.outcome: AI accuracy compared with 77 endoscopists on same videos
evidence.effect: ENDOANGEL-ED accuracy higher than all endoscopists in internal (81.10% vs. 70.61%, p<0.001) and external videos (88.24% vs. 78.49%, p<0.001).
evidence.quote: In man-machine comparison, the accuracy of ENDOANGEL-ED was significantly higher than that of all endoscopists in internal (81.10% vs. 70.61%, p < 0.001) and external videos (88.24% vs. 78.49%, p < 0.001).
evidence.sample_unit: endoscopists (man-machine comparison); dataset of 4482 images and 296 videos from 3279 patients

evidence.title: Optical Biopsy of Dysplasia in Barrett's Oesophagus Assisted by Artificial Intelligence
evidence.outcome: AI-assisted versus unassisted clinicians
evidence.effect: AI-assisted follow-up sensitivity 91.11% vs 71.11%; accuracy 82.78% vs 70.56%.
evidence.quote: AI-assisted gastroenterologists scored substantially better than unassisted gastroenterologists in establishing an optical biopsy of Barrett’s-associated dysplasia through EC.

evidence.title: Screening for extranodal extension in HPV-associated oropharyngeal carcinoma: evaluation of a CT-based deep learning algorithm in patient data from a multicentre, randomised de-escalation trial
evidence.outcome: Deep learning algorithm AUC for ENE versus four head and neck radiologists on same data
evidence.effect: Algorithm AUC 0·86 (95% CI 0·82-0·90), outperforming all readers (p<0·0001 for each); radiologist kappa 0·32.
evidence.quote: The deep learning algorithm AUC for ENE classification was 0·86 (95% CI 0·82-0·90), outperforming all readers (p<0·0001 for each).

evidence.title: Artificial intelligence for tumour tissue detection and histological regression grading in oesophageal adenocarcinomas: a retrospective algorithm development and validation study
evidence.outcome: AI regression grading compared against a group of 12 pathologists on the same retrospective cases
evidence.effect: Case-level agreement was 63·6% (quadratic kappa 0·749). AI grading triggered true reclassification in seven cases, six of which had small tumour regions initially missed by pathologists.
evidence.quote: The AI-based regression grading triggered true reclassification of resected tumour slides in seven cases (including six cases who had small tumour regions that were initially missed by pathologists).
evidence.sample_unit: pathologists compared against the AI grading (test cohorts: 320 annotated slides; 3 pathologists in the assisted-reading study)

evidence.title: Development, multi-institutional external validation, and algorithmic audit of an artificial intelligence-based Side-specific Extra-Prostatic Extension Risk Assessment tool (SEPERA) for patients undergoing radical prostatectomy: a retrospective cohort study
evidence.outcome: SEPERA performance and net benefit versus existing nomograms and logistic regression on same data
evidence.effect: SEPERA best across validation cohorts (pooled AUROC 0.77, AUPRC 0.61); higher net benefit than other models; correctly predicted ssEPE in 72 (68%) of 106 benign-biopsy cases vs 47 (44%) logistic regression, 0 Sayyid, 13 (12%) Soeterik non-MRI, 5 (5%) Soeterik MRI.
evidence.quote: SEPERA was well calibrated and had the best performance across all validation cohorts (pooled AUROC of 0·77 [95% CI 0·75-0·78] and pooled AUPRC of 0·61 [0·58-0·63]).

evidence.title: Clinical evaluation of a deep learning segmentation model including manual adjustments afterwards for locally advanced breast cancer
evidence.venue: Technical innovations & patient support in radiation oncology
evidence.outcome: Contouring time with auto-segmentation plus correction versus manual delineation on same patients
evidence.effect: Time reduction in 95% of cases; mean 42.4% ± 26.5% for OARs and 58.5% ± 19.1% for CTVs; absolute mean reduction 00:08:51 and 00:25:38.
evidence.quote: Only for one patient case out of 20, the time needed to correct the OARs took more time than the manual delineation (00:12:40 vs 00:10:15), leading to a decrease in time in 95% of the patients.

evidence.title: Retrospective batch analysis to evaluate the diagnostic accuracy of a clinically deployed AI algorithm for the detection of acute pulmonary embolism on CTPA
evidence.outcome: AI versus attending radiologist diagnostic accuracy for PE on same CTPA data
evidence.effect: AI sensitivity 96.8% vs radiologist 91.6% (p<0.001); specificity 99.9% vs 99.7% (p=0.035); AI missed 23 PE vs radiologist 60.
evidence.quote: The sensitivity for the detection of PE by the AI algorithm was significantly higher compared to the radiology report (96.8% vs. 91.6%, p < 0.001).

evidence.title: Prediction of metastatic pheochromocytoma and paraganglioma: a machine learning modelling study using data from a cross-sectional cohort
evidence.outcome: ML model AUC versus 12 specialists' predictions of metastatic disease on same data
evidence.effect: Model AUC 0.942 (95% CI 0.894-0.969) exceeded best specialist before (0.815) and after (0.812) SDHB data, p<0.0001.
evidence.quote: This model had an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0·942 (95% CI 0·894-0·969) that was larger (p<0·0001) than that of the best performing specialist before (0·815, 0·778-0·853) and after (0·812, 0·781-0·854) provision of SDHB variant data.

evidence.title: Performance of a Support Vector Machine Learning Tool for Diagnosing Diabetic Retinopathy in Clinical Practice
evidence.outcome: Software sensitivity and specificity versus routine screening grading, both compared with ophthalmologist reference grading
evidence.effect: Software sensitivity 84.9%, specificity 89.9%, PPV 92.1%, NPV 81.0%; routine grading 87.0%, 85.3%, 89.2%, 82.5%; overlapping confidence intervals; AUC 93.4%.
evidence.quote: The software performed similarly to routine grading with overlapping confidence intervals, indicating comparable performance between the two groups.

evidence.title: Added value of an artificial intelligence algorithm in reducing the number of missed incidental acute pulmonary embolism in routine portal venous phase chest CT
evidence.outcome: AI vs initial radiologist report diagnostic performance for incidental PE on same CTs
evidence.effect: Sensitivity 95.5% vs 62.7% (p<0.001); specificity 99.6% vs 99.9% (p=0.012); false positives 11 vs 2; PPV 85.3% vs 95.5% (p=0.047); AI found 25 additional unreported PE.
evidence.quote: Sensitivity of the AI algorithm was significantly higher than the outcome of the initial report (respectively 95.5% vs. 62.7%, p < 0.001), whereas specificity was very high for both (respectively 99.6% vs 99.9%, p = 0.012).
evidence.sample_unit: patients (consecutive routine portal venous chest CTs)

evidence.title: Artificial intelligence chatbot performance in triage of ophthalmic conditions
evidence.venue: Canadian journal of ophthalmology. Journal canadien d'ophtalmologie
evidence.outcome: Diagnostic accuracy of chatbots compared with ophthalmology trainees on the same vignettes
evidence.effect: Correct diagnosis in top 3: trainees 42 (95%), ChatGPT 41 (93%), Bing Chat 34 (77%), WebMD 8 (33%).
evidence.quote: The ophthalmologists in training, ChatGPT, Bing Chat, and the WebMD Symptom Checker listed the appropriate diagnosis among the top 3 suggestions in 42 (95%), 41 (93%), 34 (77%), and 8 (33%) cases, respectively.
