evidence.title: Illness severity assessment of older adults in critical illness using machine learning (ELDER-ICU): an international multicentre study with subgroup bias evaluation
evidence.outcome: Comparison of the ELDER-ICU XGBoost model against other ML algorithms and clinical scores
evidence.effect: XGBoost performed best in all validation types versus three other ML algorithms and five clinical scores; e.g., internal AUROC 0·866, external US 0·838.
evidence.quote: The final XGBoost model was compared against three other machine learning algorithms and five clinical scores.
evidence.sample_unit: patients (development 50,366; internal validation 5,037; US external 20,541; European external 2,411; temporal 4,311)

evidence.title: Predicting acute clinical deterioration with interpretable machine learning to support emergency care decision making
evidence.outcome: ML model performance versus NEWS2 baseline on the same data
evidence.effect: Up to 0.366 increase in average precision and a reduction in daily alert rate compared with NEWS2
evidence.quote: We compare model performance to the National Early Warning Score 2 (NEWS2) and yield up to a 0.366 increase in average precision, up to a [Formula: see text] reduction in daily alert rate, and a median 0.599 reduction in differential bias amplification across the protected demographics of age and sex.

evidence.title: Evaluation of inpatient medication guidance from an artificial intelligence chatbot
evidence.venue: American journal of health-system pharmacy : AJHP : official journal of the American Society of Health-System Pharmacists
evidence.outcome: Chatbot vs medication database vs pharmacists on correctness, completeness, safety, usefulness
evidence.effect: Database answered 97% of questions vs chatbot 80%; acceptable completeness 76% vs 65%, safety 83% vs 71%, usefulness 81% vs 68%; correctness 88% vs 85%.
evidence.quote: Traditional search methods using a drug database provide more clinically correct, complete, safe, and useful answers than a chatbot.

evidence.title: The potential of chatbots in chronic venous disease patient management
evidence.outcome: Comparison of candidate chatbots on identical questions graded by specialists
evidence.effect: ChatGPT 4.0 outperformed ChatGPT 3.5 on administrative questions (20/20 grade 1 vs 14/20, 70%) and on complex questions (75% vs 45% grade 1); Clinical Camel performed worst (0% grade 1).
evidence.quote: On administrative and non-complex medical questions, ChatGPT 4.0 performed better than ChatGPT 3.5.

evidence.title: GPT-4 Underperforms Experts in Detecting IV Fluid Contamination
evidence.venue: The journal of applied laboratory medicine
evidence.outcome: GPT-4 accuracy versus healthcare personnel for detecting IV fluid contamination of BMP results
evidence.effect: Accuracy 95% CI 0.57-0.71 for GPT-4 vs 0.73-0.80 for HCP on NS set; 0.57-0.57 vs 0.73-0.80 on D5NS set. GPT-4 less accurate than trained HCP.
evidence.quote: GPT-4 is less accurate than trained HCP for detecting IV fluid contamination of basic metabolic panel results.

evidence.title: External validity of an automated delirium prediction model (DEMO) and comparison to the manual VMS-questions: a retrospective cohort study
evidence.outcome: DEMO performance compared with manual VMS-questions on same admissions
evidence.effect: DEMO had lower specificity (0.64 vs. 0.72; p < 0.001) and comparable sensitivity (0.83 vs. 0.80; p = 0.56) in patients ≥70 years.
evidence.quote: Compared to the VMS-questions, the DEMO showed a lower specificity (0.64 vs. 0.72; p < 0.001) and a comparable sensitivity (0.83 vs. 0.80; p = 0.56).

evidence.title: Evaluation of a Deep Learning-based Algorithm for Post-Radiotherapy Prostate Cancer Local Recurrence Detection Using Biparametric MRI
evidence.outcome: AI detection sensitivity compared with radiologist assessment on the same patients
evidence.effect: AI was less sensitive than radiologists at patient level (76.1% vs 91.3%, p=0.02) and lesion level (71.4% vs 87.5%, p=0.01).
evidence.quote: The AI model performance was lower than the prospective radiology interpretation (Rad) on a patient-(AI: 76.1% vs. Rad: 91.3%, p = 0.02) and lesion-level (AI: 71.4% vs. Rad: 87.5%, p = 0.01).

evidence.title: Incorporation of CAD (computer-aided detection) with thin-slice lung CT in routine 18F-FDG PET/CT imaging read-out protocol for detection of lung nodules
evidence.outcome: AUC versus non-AI protocols
evidence.effect: Overall AUCs were FDG PET 0.720, lCT 0.810, dCT 0.783, and CADs 0.799; lCT, dCT, and CAD showed comparable AUCs 0.78–0.81.
evidence.quote: In summary, regarding the diagnosis of metastasis on a patient basis, PET AUC (0.72) was inferior to lCT, dCT, and CAD because of low sensitivity (48%) in all three readers, but lCT, dCT, and CAD showed comparable good results in all the readers (AUC between 0.78 and 0.81).

evidence.title: Diagnostic accuracy of a large language model in rheumatology: comparison of physician and ChatGPT-4
evidence.outcome: Correct diagnosis as top-1 and top-3 diagnoses, ChatGPT-4 versus rheumatologists on same cases
evidence.effect: Top diagnosis 35% vs 39% (p = 0.30); among top 3, 60% vs 55% (p = 0.38); higher sensitivity for IRD but lower specificity than rheumatologists.
evidence.quote: ChatGPT-4 listed the correct diagnosis comparable often to rheumatologists as the top diagnosis 35% vs 39% (p = 0.30); as well as among the top 3 diagnoses, 60% vs 55%, (p = 0.38).

evidence.title: Enhanced YOLOv5 network-based object detection (BALFilter Reader) promotes PERFECT filter-enabled liquid biopsy of lung cancer from bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF)
evidence.outcome: Diagnostic performance of AI versus two experienced pathologists on same clinical cases, histopathology as gold standard
evidence.effect: BALFilter Reader sensitivity 66.7% ± 16.7%, specificity 100.0% ± 0.0%, accuracy 75.0% ± 12.5% in ~2 min, versus pathologists' sensitivity 61.1%, specificity 16.7%, accuracy 50.0% in 10-30 min.
evidence.quote: The overall diagnosis performance (~2 min) with sensitivity@66.7% ± 16.7%, specificity@100.0% ± 0.0% and accuracy@75.0% ± 12.5% was superior to that from two experienced pathologists (10-30 min) with sensitivity@61.1%, specificity@16.7% and accuracy@50.0%, with the histopathological result as the gold standard.

evidence.title: Generative Artificial Intelligence for Chest Radiograph Interpretation in the Emergency Department
evidence.outcome: ED physician Likert ratings of AI vs radiologist vs teleradiology chest radiograph reports
evidence.effect: AI (mean 3.22) and radiologist (3.34) reports scored significantly higher than teleradiology (2.74; P<.001); AI and radiologist not significantly different.
evidence.quote: There was a significant association of report type with ratings, with post hoc tests revealing significantly greater scores for AI (mean [SE] score, 3.22 [0.34]; P < .001) and radiologist (mean [SE] score, 3.34 [0.34]; P < .001) reports compared with teleradiology (mean [SE] score, 2.74 [0.34]) reports.

evidence.title: Evaluating the reliability of ChatGPT as a tool for imaging test referral: a comparative study with a clinical decision support system
evidence.outcome: Agreement of ChatGPT imaging referral recommendations with ESR iGuide clinical decision support on same cases
evidence.effect: ChatGPT recommendations were consistent with ESR iGuide; disagreement in 12.4% of cases; high agreement between ChatGPT and specialists on CAP CT cases (n=66).
evidence.quote: ChatGPT recommendations were consistent with the recommendations provided by the ESR iGuide.
evidence.sample_unit: emergency department cases with abdominal complaints

evidence.title: Comparison of clinical utility of deep learning-based systems for small-bowel capsule endoscopy reading
evidence.outcome: Head-to-head comparison of two CNN systems' clinical utility on the same SBCE videos
evidence.effect: Both systems extracted all 43 lesions. The novel CNN captured 9.4% of images vs 24.3% for the existing one, giving the shortest reading time (10.1 vs 23.1 min).
evidence.quote: CNN performance directly affects clinical utility and should be carefully assessed.

evidence.title: Can the generalizability issue of artificial intelligence be overcome? Pneumothorax detection algorithm
evidence.venue: Journal of investigative medicine : the official publication of the American Federation for Clinical Research
evidence.outcome: Algorithm sensitivity/specificity compared with physicians on the same test data
evidence.effect: Physicians' sensitivity 0.585 and specificity 0.988; algorithms detected 49/50 pneumothoraces (sensitivity 0.98) but with more false positives (PDA-Alpha 7, PDA-Beta 1).
evidence.quote: The physicians' sensitivity and specificity for detecting pneumothorax were 0.585 and 0.988, respectively.

evidence.title: A real-world clinical validation for AI-based MRI monitoring in multiple sclerosis
evidence.outcome: Case-level sensitivity for new/enlarging lesions, AI tool vs standard radiology reports, against consensus ground truth
evidence.effect: AI tool sensitivity 93.3% vs 58.3% for radiology reports, with minimal loss of specificity; AI equivalent to a core trial imaging lab for lesion activity and brain volume (PBVC -0.32% vs -0.36%).
evidence.quote: In 397 multi-center MRI scan pairs acquired in routine practice, we demonstrate superior case-level sensitivity of a clinically integrated AI-based tool over standard radiology reports (93.3% vs 58.3%), relative to a consensus ground truth, with minimal loss of specificity.

evidence.title: Framework for Radiation Oncology Department-wide Evaluation and Implementation of Commercial Artificial Intelligence Autocontouring
evidence.outcome: Head-to-head comparison of three commercial autocontouring products on same patient data
evidence.effect: AI1/AI2/AI3 differed by disease site; e.g., brain median DSC 0.65/0.78/0.75; qualitative acceptability 70.7% (AI1) and 74.6% (AI2) of ROIs.
evidence.quote: Qualitatively, AI1 and AI2 contours were acceptable (rated 1-2) with at most minor edits in 70.7% and 74.6% of ROIs (2906 ratings), higher for abdomen (AI1: 79.2%) and thorax (AI2: 90.2%), and lower for H&N (29.0/35.6%).
evidence.sample_unit: patient planning CT scans (859 clinically approved contours)

evidence.title: Population-wide evaluation of artificial intelligence and radiologist assessment of screening mammograms
evidence.outcome: Standalone AI vs first-reader radiologists on cancer detection accuracy, same data
evidence.effect: AI matched at first-reader specificity was comparable on all measures (sensitivity 62.6% vs 63.5%, p=0.43); AI matched at sensitivity had lower specificity (97.5% vs 97.7%) and higher recall rate; different cancers detected.
evidence.quote: Standalone AI spec did not differ statistically significantly from the first reader across any accuracy measures (Table 2 ).

evidence.title: ChatGPT versus clinician: challenging the diagnostic capabilities of artificial intelligence in dermatology
evidence.outcome: Diagnostic accuracy of ChatGPT versus nonspecialist referrers and dermatologists on same cases
evidence.effect: ChatGPT correct 56% with dermatologist-recorded data and 39% with nonspecialist-recorded data; nonspecialists 36%; dermatologists 83% (n=30).
evidence.quote: This was similar to the diagnostic rate of nonspecialists (36%; n = 13), but it was much lower than that of dermatologists (83%; n = 30).

evidence.title: Operational greenhouse-gas emissions of deep learning in digital pathology: a modelling study
evidence.outcome: RCC-classification accuracy and operational emissions
evidence.effect: VGG16 outperformed ConvNeXt while reducing CO2eq emissions by approximately 8 times.
evidence.quote: Despite having fewer trainable parameters, VGG16, a relatively simple deep-learning model, outperformed ConvNeXt, a deeper model, while reducing CO 2 eq emissions by approximately 8 times ( figure 4A ; appendix pp 21–22 ).
evidence.sample_unit: whole-slide images (slides digitised from 13 breast and prostate cancer cases)

evidence.title: A newly developed deep learning-based system for automatic detection and classification of small bowel lesions during double-balloon enteroscopy examination
evidence.outcome: AI accuracy compared with 8 endoscopists on same video test set
evidence.effect: System accuracy 85% vs endoscopists 77 ± 6% (p < 0.01); superior to novices and comparable to experts.
evidence.quote: For the video test set, the accuracy of the system was significantly better than that of the endoscopists (85% vs. 77 ± 6%, p < 0.01).
evidence.sample_unit: videos from independent patients (test set); also 1318 normal and 915 abnormal images

evidence.title: Comparing Artificial Intelligence and Senior Residents in Oral Lesion Diagnosis: A Comparative Study
evidence.outcome: LLM versus senior resident scores on oral lesion diagnosis multiple-choice test
evidence.effect: Median LLM score 50.0 (45.0-60.0) vs residents 65.0 (55.0-75.0); no significant difference (p = 0.211).
evidence.quote: There was no significant difference in the percent scores of residents and LLMs (p = 0.211).
evidence.sample_unit: residents and 20 multiple-choice oral lesion questions

evidence.title: Assessing the clinical reasoning of ChatGPT for mechanical thrombectomy in patients with stroke
evidence.outcome: ChatGPT thrombectomy decisions compared with board-certified stroke neurologists and neurointerventionalists on same patients
evidence.effect: ChatGPT agreed with the physician's decision whether or not to pursue thrombectomy in 54.3% of cases; mistakes in 8.8% of cases.
evidence.quote: ChatGPT agreed with the physician's decision whether or not to pursue thrombectomy in 54.3% of the cases.
evidence.sample_unit: patients with large vessel occlusion who underwent mechanical thrombectomy

evidence.title: Validation of a Deep Learning Chest X-ray Interpretation Model: Integrating Large-Scale AI and Large Language Models for Comparative Analysis with ChatGPT
evidence.outcome: Comparison of candidate AI systems on same chest X-ray data for accuracy
evidence.effect: KARA-CXR rated 'Acceptable' 70.50% and 68.00% by two observers vs ChatGPT 40.50% and 47.00%; KARA-CXR significantly more accurate.
evidence.quote: In the 'Acceptable' accuracy category, KARA-CXR was rated at 70.50% and 68.00% by two observers, while ChatGPT achieved 40.50% and 47.00%.

evidence.title: Potential impact of a new sepsis prediction model for the primary care setting: early health economic evaluation using an observational cohort
evidence.outcome: Cost per patient of model-guided referral versus usual GP care
evidence.effect: Model-based referral cost €5954-€6742 per patient vs €5890 observed; probabilistic analysis showed higher model costs than usual care in 83% of runs.
evidence.quote: In the probabilistic sensitivity analyses, costs for the prediction model were higher than usual care in 83% of the runs ( figure 3 ).

evidence.title: Interpretable artificial intelligence-based app assists inexperienced radiologists in diagnosing biliary atresia from sonographic gallbladder images
evidence.outcome: AI model diagnostic AUC compared with radiologists and previous model on same data
evidence.effect: New model AUC 0.860 vs experienced radiologists 0.876, junior 0.773, senior 0.749; outperformed prior model on external set (AUC 0.924 vs 0.908, P = 0.004).
evidence.quote: When tested in real-world mimic settings using 333 sonographic gallbladder videos, the new model performed comparable to experienced pediatric radiologists (average AUC 0.860 vs 0.876) and outperformed junior radiologists (average AUC 0.838 vs 0.773) and senior radiologists (average AUC 0.829 vs 0.749).
evidence.sample_unit: prospectively collected sonographic gallbladder videos (from 207 infants) read by 18 radiologists

evidence.title: Large-Scale assessment of ChatGPT's performance in benign and malignant bone tumors imaging report diagnosis and its potential for clinical applications
evidence.outcome: ChatGPT diagnostic accuracy, sensitivity, specificity versus physicians on same reports
evidence.effect: Physicians: accuracy 0.88, sensitivity 0.99, specificity 0.81, AUC 0.92; ChatGPT direct: 0.73, 0.95, 0.58, AUC 0.72; few-shot: 0.87, 0.99, 0.73, AUC 0.83; physicians statistically superior (P=0.0008).
evidence.quote: Additionally, the comparison between physicians and few-shot enhanced ChatGPT showed a T-statistic of 3.42 with a P-value of 0.0008, underscoring the physicians' statistically superior performance.

evidence.title: Comparing the Quality of Domain-Specific Versus General Language Models for Artificial Intelligence-Generated Differential Diagnoses in PICU Patients
evidence.venue: Pediatric critical care medicine : a journal of the Society of Critical Care Medicine and the World Federation of Pediatric Intensive and Critical Care Societies
evidence.outcome: Expert-rated quality of LM differential diagnoses compared with clinician-written ones on same notes
evidence.effect: Clinicians scored 3.43 vs 2.88 for fine-tuned LLaMa-7B, the best LM (difference 0.54, 95% CI 0.37-0.72, p<0.001). Clinicians ranked highest in 55% of cases, LLaMa-7B in 29%.
evidence.quote: The mean quality scores of the differential diagnoses generated by the clinicians and fine-tuned LLaMa-7B, the best-performing LM, were 3.43 and 2.88, respectively (absolute difference 0.54 units [95% CI, 0.37-0.72], p < 0.001).

evidence.title: Exploring the role of ChatGPT in clinical decision-making in otorhinolaryngology: a ChatGPT designed study
evidence.venue: European archives of oto-rhino-laryngology : official journal of the European Federation of Oto-Rhino-Laryngological Societies (EUFOS) : affiliated with the German Society for Oto-Rhino-Laryngology - Head and Neck Surgery
evidence.outcome: ChatGPT agreement scores compared with otorhinolaryngologists on same cases
evidence.effect: ChatGPT-1 mean 4.4 (SD 1.2), ChatGPT-2 4.15 (SD 1.3), ENTs 4.91 (SD 0.3); Mann-Whitney U p < 0.001.
evidence.quote: The Mann-Whitney U test revealed a statistically significant difference (p < 0.001) between both ChatGPT's and the ENTs's score.

evidence.title: Smartphone AI vs. Medical Experts: A Comparative Study in Prehospital STEMI Diagnosis
evidence.outcome: AI STEMI biomarker vs expert consensus sensitivity and specificity non-inferiority
evidence.effect: AUC 0.815 vs 0.736 (p=0.081); sensitivity difference 0.042 (-0.099-0.182), specificity difference 0.103 (-0.043-0.250); non-inferiority confirmed with 0.100 margin
evidence.quote: The 95% confidence interval of sensitivity and specificity differences between qSTEMI and consensus score were 0.042 (-0.099-0.182) and 0.103 (-0.043-0.250), respectively, confirming qSTEMI's non-inferiority.

evidence.title: Optimizing warfarin dosing for patients with atrial fibrillation using machine learning
evidence.outcome: Compared RL warfarin dosing model against rules-based algorithm for TTR and composite clinical outcome
evidence.effect: RL: each 10% increase in algorithm-consistent dosing gave 6.78% TTR improvement and HR 0.89; rules-based benchmark gave 6.10% TTR improvement and HR 0.90, so results were comparable.
evidence.quote: These results were comparable to those of a rules-based clinical algorithm used for benchmarking, for which each 10% increase in algorithm-consistent dosing independently predicted a 6.10% increase in TTR (95% CI 5.67, 6.54, p < 0.001) and a 10% decrease in the composite outcome (HR 0.90; 95% CI 0.83, 0.98, p = 0.018).

evidence.title: ChatGPT vs. web search for patient questions: what does ChatGPT do better?
evidence.venue: European archives of oto-rhino-laryngology : official journal of the European Federation of Oto-Rhino-Laryngological Societies (EUFOS) : affiliated with the German Society for Oto-Rhino-Laryngology - Head and Neck Surgery
evidence.outcome: accuracy versus web search by question category
evidence.effect: Higher for Diagnosis (p < 0.01); no difference for Fact (p = 0.15) or Policy (p = 0.22).
evidence.quote: ChatGPT scored higher than web search for questions the 'Diagnosis' category (p < 0.01); there was no difference in questions categorized as 'Fact' (p = 0.15) or 'Policy' (p = 0.22).

evidence.title: Exploring the use of ChatGPT in predicting anterior circulation stroke functional outcomes after mechanical thrombectomy: a pilot study
evidence.outcome: Agreement of dichotomized 3-month mRS predictions with actual outcomes, ChatGPT versus MT-DRAGON score
evidence.effect: ChatGPT showed fair (κ=0.354) exact and good (κ=0.727) dichotomized agreement with true mRS, outperforming MT-DRAGON in overall and subgroup predictions.
evidence.quote: ChatGPT demonstrated fair (κ=0.354, 95% CI 0.260 to 0.448) and good (κ=0.727, 95% CI 0.620 to 0.833) agreement with the true exact and dichotomized mRS scores at 3 months, respectively, outperforming MT-DRAGON in overall and subgroup predictions.

evidence.title: Clinical decision support for bipolar depression using large language models
evidence.venue: Neuropsychopharmacology : official publication of the American College of Neuropsychopharmacology
evidence.outcome: Augmented LLM versus community clinicians and base model on expert-defined optimal choice
evidence.effect: Augmented model 50.8% optimal vs community clinicians 23.1% (McNemar p<0.001) and base model 23.4%.
evidence.quote: A sample of community clinicians scoring the same vignettes identified the optimal choice for 23.1% (95% CI 15.7-30.5%) of vignettes, on average; McNemar's p < 0.001 versus augmented model.
evidence.sample_unit: clinical vignettes (each run 20 times, 1000 model outputs per condition)

evidence.title: Accuracy and consistency of chatbots versus clinicians for answering pediatric dentistry questions: A pilot study
evidence.outcome: Accuracy of chatbots versus pediatric dentists, general dentists, and students on the same questions
evidence.effect: Pediatric dentists 96.67%±4.3%, general dentists 88.0%±6.1%, students 80.8%±6.9%; best chatbot (ChatGPT) 78%±3%; clinicians significantly more accurate than chatbots (p<0.001).
evidence.quote: General dentists (88.0 % ± 6.1 %) also demonstrated significantly higher accuracy than chatbots (p < 0.001), followed by students (80.8 %±6.9 %).
evidence.sample_unit: true/false pediatric dentistry questions (answered by 9 chatbots x 3 conversations and 60 clinicians)

evidence.title: A Comparative Study of Large Language Models, Human Experts, and Expert-Edited Large Language Models to Neuro-Ophthalmology Questions
evidence.venue: Journal of neuro-ophthalmology : the official journal of the North American Neuro-Ophthalmology Society
evidence.outcome: Expert-rated quality of LLM responses versus human expert responses on the same questions
evidence.effect: Quality: Expert + AI 4.16, GPT-4 4.04, GPT-3.5 3.99, Claude 3.6, Expert 3.56, Bard 3.5, Bing 3.04; differences significant (P<0.0001).
evidence.quote: For quality, Expert + AI (4.16 ± 0.81) performed the best, followed by GPT-4 (4.04 ± 0.92), GPT-3.5 (3.99 ± 0.87), Claude (3.6 ± 1.09), Expert (3.56 ± 1.01), Bard (3.5 ± 1.15), and Bing (3.04 ± 1.12).

evidence.title: Examining the reliability of brain age algorithms under varying degrees of participant motion
evidence.outcome: Comparative reliability and robustness of five brain age algorithms on the same motion-varied MRI data
evidence.effect: DeepBrainNet and pyment showed greatest robustness (ICCs 0.956-0.965); XGBoost and brainageR had largest errors (up to 13.5 RMSE) and bias with motion.
evidence.quote: DeepBrainNet and pyment showed greatest robustness and reliability (ICCs = 0.956-0.965).
evidence.sample_unit: participants (adults with MRI scans under no, low, and high motion conditions)

evidence.title: A Retrospective Comparison of Medication Recommendations Between a Cardiologist and ChatGPT-4 for Hypertension Patients in a Rural Clinic
evidence.outcome: Agreement of GPT-4 hypertension medication recommendations with cardiologist recommendations on same patient data
evidence.effect: 95% of 40 patients had conflicting overall recommendations; only 10.2% of specific medication recommendations matched; Cohen's kappa -0.0127 (no agreement).
evidence.quote: Out of the 40 patients, 95% had conflicting overall recommendations between the physician and GPT-4, with only 10.2% of the specific medication recommendations matching between the two.

evidence.title: An artificial intelligence model for detecting pathological lymph node metastasis in prostate cancer using whole slide images: a retrospective, multicentre, diagnostic study
evidence.outcome: AI sensitivity compared with junior and senior pathologists on the same data
evidence.effect: AI sensitivity 0.983 exceeded two junior pathologists (0.862, P=0.023; 0.879, P=0.041) by 10-12% and matched two senior pathologists (both 0.983).
evidence.quote: In the human-AI comparison and collaboration study, the sensitivity of ProCaLNMD (0.983 [0.908-1.000]) surpassed that of two junior pathologists (0.862 [0.746-0.939], P = 0.023; 0.879 [0.767-0.950], P = 0.041) by 10-12% and showed no difference to that of two senior pathologists (both 0.983 [0.908-1.000], both P > 0.99).
evidence.sample_unit: patients with prostate cancer (8158 slides, 18,761 lymph nodes)

evidence.title: Data Extraction from Free-Text Reports on Mechanical Thrombectomy in Acute Ischemic Stroke Using ChatGPT: A Retrospective Analysis
evidence.outcome: Correct data extraction by GPT-4 versus GPT-3.5 on the same reports against manual reference standard
evidence.effect: GPT-4 extracted 2631 of 2800 entries correctly (94.0%) vs GPT-3.5 1788 of 2800 (63.9%), P<.001; external reports 90.5% vs 64.2%, P<.001.
evidence.quote: With 1788 of 2800 correct data entries, GPT-3.5 produced fewer correct data entries than did GPT-4 (63.9% [95% CI: 62.0, 65.6]; range per category, 14%-99%; P < .001).

evidence.title: Potential of GPT-4 for Detecting Errors in Radiology Reports: Implications for Reporting Accuracy
evidence.outcome: GPT-4 error detection rate versus radiologists on the same reports
evidence.effect: GPT-4 detected 82.7% (124/150) of errors, matching average radiologist performance (80.0% to 89.3%; P range .522-.99); one senior radiologist outperformed GPT-4 (94.7%, P=.006).
evidence.quote: GPT-4 (detection rate, 82.7%;124 of 150; 95% CI: 75.8, 87.9) matched the average detection performance of radiologists independent of their experience (senior radiologists, 89.3% [134 of 150; 95% CI: 83.4, 93.3]; attending physicians, 80.0% [120 of 150; 95% CI: 72.9, 85.6]; residents, 80.0% [120 of 150; 95% CI: 72.9, 85.6]; P value range, .522-.99).

evidence.title: Validation of GPT-4 for clinical event classification: A comparative analysis with ICD codes and human reviewers
evidence.outcome: GPT-4 accuracy versus ICD codes and human reviewers for GI bleeding classification on same data
evidence.effect: GPT-4 accuracy 94.4% vs ICD codes 63.5% (P<0.001); vs Reviewer 1 98.5% (P<0.001); vs Reviewer 2 90.8% (P=0.170).
evidence.quote: GPT-4 exhibited an accuracy of 94.4% in identifying GI bleeding occurrences, outperforming ICD codes (accuracy 63.5%, P < 0.001).

evidence.title: A Comparative Study of Responses to Retina Questions from Either Experts, Expert-Edited Large Language Models, or Expert-Edited Large Language Models Alone
evidence.outcome: LLM responses compared against expert-written responses on quality, empathy, safety
evidence.effect: ChatGPT-3.5 and ChatGPT-4 scored higher than Expert in quality (P < 0.001); ChatGPT-4 was similar to Expert on safety metrics, and better on missing content (P = 0.001).
evidence.quote: Comparing the top LLM (ChatGPT-4) versus Expert demonstrates that the LLM performed similarly (inappropriate and/or incorrect content P = 0.35; extent of possible harm P = 0.356; likelihood of possible harm P = 0.129); or better missing content ( P = 0.001) ( Table 8 ).

evidence.title: Use of a Large Language Model to Assess Clinical Acuity of Adults in the Emergency Department
evidence.outcome: LLM accuracy vs physician reviewer and earlier LLM in identifying higher-acuity patient
evidence.effect: GPT-4 accuracy 0.89 vs comparator LLM 0.84 (10,000 pairs); in 500-pair subsample LLM 0.88 vs physician reviewer 0.86.
evidence.quote: Among the 500-pair subsample that was also manually classified, LLM performance (accuracy, 0.88 [95% CI, 0.86-0.91]) was comparable with that of the physician reviewer (accuracy, 0.86 [95% CI, 0.83-0.89]).

evidence.title: Comparative analysis of ChatGPT, Gemini and emergency medicine specialist in ESI triage assessment
evidence.venue: The American journal of emergency medicine
evidence.outcome: Triage accuracy of candidate LLMs compared with emergency medicine specialists on the same cases
evidence.effect: GPT-4 had the highest correct triage rate; in ESI 1-2, Gemini 87.77% and GPT-4 85.11% versus specialists 49.33% correct.
evidence.quote: In the ESI 1-2 class, Gemini had a correct triage rate of 87.77%, GPT-4 had 85.11%, and emergency medicine specialists had 49.33%.

evidence.title: ChatGPT4 Outperforms Endoscopists for Determination of Postcolonoscopy Rescreening and Surveillance Recommendations
evidence.venue: Clinical gastroenterology and hepatology : the official clinical practice journal of the American Gastroenterological Association
evidence.outcome: Agreement of ChatGPT4 vs endoscopist recommendations with USMSTF guideline panel
evidence.effect: ChatGPT4 agreed with USMSTF Panel in 85.7% vs 75.4% for gastroenterology practice (P < .001).
evidence.quote: ChatGPT4 recommendations were in closer agreement with the USMSTF Panel (85.7%) than gastroenterology practice recommendations with the USMSTF Panel (75.4%) (P < .001).

evidence.title: Establishment and validation of an artificial intelligence web application for predicting postoperative in-hospital mortality in patients with hip fracture: a national cohort study of 52 707 cases
evidence.outcome: Predictive AUC of AI application versus doctors and versus simpler models on same data
evidence.effect: AI application AUC 0.908 vs doctors 0.682 (P<0.001); eXGBM scored highest (56) among six models, above logistic regression (27).
evidence.quote: The comparative testing revealed that the AI application's predictive capabilities significantly outperformed those of the doctors in terms of AUC values (0.908 vs. 0.682, P <0.001).

evidence.title: Safety and quality of AI chatbots for drug-related inquiries: A real-world comparison with licensed pharmacists
evidence.outcome: Accuracy, detail, and risk of harm of GPT chatbots versus licensed pharmacists on same inquiries
evidence.effect: GPT-4 had 64.3% completely accurate responses, comparable to human pharmacists; both delivered 95% safe responses; GPT-4 gave proactive risk mitigation info in 70% vs 25.7% for pharmacists.
evidence.quote: GPT-4 had 64.3% completely accurate responses, comparable to human pharmacists.

evidence.title: Accuracy of artificial intelligence-based segmentation of the mandibular canal in CBCT
evidence.outcome: Accuracy (RMS error) and time of AI vs manual tracing by clinicians of differing experience
evidence.effect: RMS error vs experienced clinicians ranged 0.21 to 7.65 mm, mean 3.5 mm; experienced manual tracing required more time than AI-driven segmentation.
evidence.quote: Regarding time efficiency, tracing by experienced users required more time compared to AI-driven segmentation.

evidence.title: Deep learning for colorectal cancer detection in contrast-enhanced CT without bowel preparation: a retrospective, multicentre study
evidence.outcome: DL model performance compared with radiologists on the same test data
evidence.effect: DL accuracy exceeded radiologists in internal (97.2% vs 86.0%) and external set 1 (94.9% vs 85.3%), p<0.0001; in real-world set sensitivity was comparable (94.3% vs 96.2%).
evidence.quote: In the real-world test set, the DL model delivered sensitivity comparable to that of radiologists who had been informed about clinical indications for most cancer cases (94.3% vs 96.2%, p > 0.99), and it detected 2 cases that had been missed by radiologists.
evidence.sample_unit: CT scans (cancer vs normal across internal, two external, and real-world test sets)

evidence.title: Large Language Models Versus Expert Clinicians in Crisis Prediction Among Telemental Health Patients: Comparative Study
evidence.outcome: GPT-4 versus 6 clinicians on predicting suicidal ideation with plan from intake data
evidence.effect: Chief complaint only: clinician precision 0.7 vs GPT-4 0.6; sensitivity 0.53 vs 0.62. Adding attempt history: clinician sensitivity 0.59, precision 0.77; GPT-4 sensitivity 0.59, precision 0.54.
evidence.quote: Overall, the clinicians' average precision (0.7) was higher than that of GPT-4 (0.6) in identifying the SI with plan at intake (n=140) versus no SI (n=200) when using the chief complaint alone, while sensitivity was higher for the GPT-4 (0.62) than the clinicians' average (0.53).

evidence.title: Optimal use of β-lactams in neonates: machine learning-based clinical decision support system
evidence.outcome: ML CDSS accuracy, precision, recall, F1 versus PopPK model on same real-world data
evidence.effect: Compared with the PopPK model, overall accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-Score improved by 10.7%, 22.1%, 64.2%, and 43.1%, respectively.
evidence.quote: Compared with the PopPK model, the overall accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-Score improved by 10.7%, 22.1%, 64.2%, and 43.1%, respectively.
evidence.sample_unit: neonates (real-world validation; count not reported in text)

evidence.title: ChatGPT-4 Performs Clinical Information Retrieval Tasks Using Consistently More Trustworthy Resources Than Does Google Search for Queries Concerning the Latarjet Procedure
evidence.venue: Arthroscopy : the journal of arthroscopic & related surgery : official publication of the Arthroscopy Association of North America and the International Arthroscopy Association
evidence.outcome: Accuracy of numeric answers from ChatGPT-4 versus Google Search, rated by blinded surgeons
evidence.effect: Mean accuracy 2.9 ± 0.9 for ChatGPT-4 versus 2.5 ± 1.4 for Google (P = .65); no significant difference, though ChatGPT-4 used only academic sources versus 30% for Google (P = .003).
evidence.quote: Mean (± standard deviation) accuracy to numeric-based answers was 2.9 ± 0.9 for ChatGPT-4 versus 2.5 ± 1.4 for Google (P = .65).

evidence.title: Artificial intelligence chatbot vs pathology faculty and residents: Real-world clinical questions from a genitourinary treatment planning conference
evidence.outcome: AI chatbot accuracy and clinical relevance score versus pathology faculty and residents on same questions
evidence.effect: Faculty 4.75, chatbot 4.10, research-prepared residents 3.50, unprepared residents 2.87; chatbot significantly better than unprepared residents (P=.03), not different from faculty (P=.30).
evidence.quote: The AI chatbot scored statistically significantly better than unprepared residents (P = .03) but not statistically significantly different from research-prepared residents (P = .33) or faculty (P = .30).

evidence.title: Real-World Application of Artificial Intelligence for Detecting Pathologic Gastric Atypia and Neoplastic Lesions
evidence.outcome: Diagnostic accuracy of AI versus initial biopsy for dysplasia/EGC in internal video set
evidence.effect: ENAD CAD-G accuracy 88.57% (dysplasia) and 91.43% (EGC) versus 60.71% for initial biopsy results (P<0.001).
evidence.quote: In the Internal video set, ENAD CAD-G identified dysplasia and EGC with diagnostic accuracies of 88.57% (95% CI, 83.30%-93.84%) and 91.43% (86.79%-96.07%), respectively, compared with an accuracy of 60.71% (52.62%-68.80%) for the initial biopsy results (P<0.001).
evidence.sample_unit: patients (154 referred atypia + 140 internal video + 296 external video)

evidence.title: Reshaping free-text radiology notes into structured reports with generative question answering transformers
evidence.outcome: Information extraction performance of fine-tuned IT5 versus GPT-3.5 on same reports
evidence.effect: Fine-tuned IT5 with batch splitting and ex-post combination performed on par with GPT-3.5 across item types; GPT-3.5 was better at plausible human-like free-text statements.
evidence.quote: The combination of fine-tuning and batch splitting allows IT5 ex-post combination to achieve notable results in terms of information extraction of different types of structured data, performing on par with GPT-3.5.
evidence.sample_unit: Italian free-text radiology reports (CT staging of lymphoma)

evidence.title: Racial Differences in Accuracy of Predictive Models for High-Flow Nasal Cannula Failure in COVID-19
evidence.outcome: Discrimination of ML models versus ROX index for HFNC failure
evidence.effect: XGB AUROC 0.707 was the only model significantly better than the ROX index (AUROC 0.616).
evidence.quote: eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGB) model had the highest area under the receiver-operator characteristic curve (AUROC) for predicting HFNC failure (0.707), and was the only model with significantly better performance than the ROX index (AUROC 0.616).

evidence.title: The Performance of ChatGPT-4 and Gemini Ultra 1.0 for Quality Assurance Review in Emergency Medical Services Chest Pain Calls
evidence.outcome: LLM agreement with expert human reviewers on EMS quality assurance metrics on the same records
evidence.effect: ChatGPT-4 had 76.2% agreement (kappa 0.401) with human reviewers on EKG documentation and aspirin administration, varying across other metrics. Gemini Ultra was discontinued due to poor performance.
evidence.quote: Gemini Ultra's evaluation was discontinued due to poor performance.
evidence.sample_unit: anonymized prehospital EMS patient care records

evidence.title: Assessing GPT-4's Performance in Delivering Medical Advice: Comparative Analysis With Human Experts
evidence.outcome: Cardiologist preference and accuracy grading of GPT-4 versus human expert answers to the same questions
evidence.effect: GPT-4 better in 132/251 (52.6%) vs human expert better in 119/251 (47.4%); humans had more high-accuracy (21.1% vs 12.6%) and more low-accuracy responses (4.6% vs 0.4%; P=.001).
evidence.quote: GPT-4 and human experts displayed comparable efficacy in medical accuracy ("GPT-4 is better" at 132/251, 52.6% vs "Human expert is better" at 119/251, 47.4%).

evidence.title: The clinical value of artificial intelligence in assisting junior radiologists in thyroid ultrasound: a multicenter prospective study from real clinical practice
evidence.outcome: diagnostic performance of AI versus clinicians
evidence.effect: AI demonstrated superior AUC compared to junior radiologists (0.901 vs. 0.829) and comparable AUC to senior radiologists (0.901 vs. 0.892).
evidence.quote: Summing over all cases which were analyzed separately using either pathology or the arbitration committee as the diagnostic criteria, or in our proposed term, the 2e diagnostic criteria, the AI system demonstrated superior sensitivity, specificity, accuracy, and AUC compared to junior radiologists (0.868 vs. 0.820, 0.934 vs. 0.837, 0.917 vs. 0.833, 0.901 vs. 0.829, respectively; all p < 0.001), and showed comparable results to senior radiologists’ readings (0.868 vs. 0.849, 0.934 vs. 0.934, 0.917 vs. 0.912, 0.901 vs. 0.892, respectively; all p > 0.05).

evidence.title: Development and evaluation of a large language model of ophthalmology in Chinese
evidence.outcome: Diagnostic accuracy of the LLM versus ophthalmologists on clinical vignettes
evidence.effect: Ophthalmologists' correct diagnosis rate was 96.1% vs 81.1% for MOPH, described as not statistically significant (p>0.05).
evidence.quote: In diagnostic accuracy, although the rate of correct diagnosis by ophthalmologists was superior to that by MOPH (96.1% vs 81.1%, p>0.05), the difference was not statistically significant.
evidence.sample_unit: exam questions, evidence-based questions, and clinical vignettes

evidence.title: Assessing breast disease with deep learning model using bimodal bi-view ultrasound images and clinical information
evidence.outcome: AI diagnostic performance compared with six radiologists on same data
evidence.effect: BreNet AUC 0.996 vs. radiologists 0.841.
evidence.quote: The diagnostic performance of BreNet was superior to that of the radiologists (area under the curve [AUC]: 0.996 vs. 0.841).

evidence.title: Comparison of the Quality of Discharge Letters Written by Large Language Models and Junior Clinicians: Single-Blinded Study
evidence.outcome: GPT-4 letter quality compared against junior clinicians on same case records
evidence.effect: GPT-4 outperformed on information provision (P=.03); equivalent on clarity (P=.12), collegiality (P=.05), conciseness (P=.71), follow-up (P=.08), overall satisfaction (P=.36).
evidence.quote: Discharge letters written by GPT-4 had equivalent quality to those written by junior clinicians, without any hallucinations.
evidence.sample_unit: letter ratings (5 cases rated by primary care physicians, GPT-4 vs junior clinician letters)

evidence.title: The diagnostic and triage accuracy of the GPT-3 artificial intelligence model: an observational study
evidence.outcome: GPT-3 diagnostic and triage accuracy compared with physicians and laypeople on same vignettes
evidence.effect: Diagnosis top-3: GPT-3 88% vs lay 54% (p<0.0001) vs physicians 96% (p=0.012). Triage: GPT-3 70% vs lay 74% (p=0.60) vs physicians 91% (p<0.0001).
evidence.quote: GPT-3 triaged 70% correct (34/48, 57-82) versus 74% (3706/5000, 73-75; p=0.60) for lay individuals and 91% (608/666, 89-93%; p<0.0001) for physicians.

evidence.title: Vignette-based comparative analysis of ChatGPT and specialist treatment decisions for rheumatic patients: results of the Rheum2Guide study
evidence.outcome: Blinded rater preference and quality ratings of LLM plans versus clinical rheumatology board plans
evidence.effect: Raters preferred the board's plans in 68.8% (110/160) versus GPT-4 16.3% (26/160) and GPT-3.5 15.0% (24/160); board plans rated significantly higher on guideline adherence, appropriateness, completeness and quality.
evidence.quote: In 68.8% (110/160) of cases, raters preferred the RB's treatment plans over those generated by GPT-4 (16.3%; 26/160) and GPT-3.5 (15.0%; 24/160).
evidence.sample_unit: ratings (20 fictional vignettes rated by 4 rheumatologists)

evidence.title: Generalizability of electroencephalographic interpretation using artificial intelligence: An external validation study
evidence.outcome: AI diagnostic accuracy compared with three blinded experts on same EEG data
evidence.effect: Overall accuracy 92% (95% CI 90%-94%) for SCORE-AI versus 94% (95% CI 92%-96%) for experts; no significant difference for any metric or category.
evidence.quote: SCORE-AI performed equally well compared to the experts, with an overall accuracy of 92% (95% confidence interval [CI] = 90%-94%) versus 94% (95% CI = 92%-96%).

evidence.title: Bridging the Gap: Can Large Language Models Match Human Expertise in Writing Neurosurgical Operative Notes?
evidence.outcome: Rated accuracy, content and organization of AI vs surgeon-written operative notes on the same cases
evidence.effect: AI accuracy 4.44 vs surgeon 4.33 (P = 0.512); AI content lower, 3.73 vs 4.42 (P < 0.001).
evidence.quote: The mean AI accuracy was not different from the mean surgeon accuracy (4.44 vs. 4.33; P = 0.512), the mean AI content was lower than the mean surgeon content (3.73 vs. 4.42; P < 0.001).
evidence.sample_unit: surveys of surgeon- or AI-written operative notes

evidence.title: Evaluating cognitive performance: Traditional methods vs. ChatGPT
evidence.outcome: memory evaluation scores
evidence.effect: GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 scores differed significantly (p<0.001), and GPT-4 showed no significant difference from physician scores (p=0.8).
evidence.quote: There was a significant difference in GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 group scores ( P < 0.001), while there was no significant difference in GPT-4 and physician group scores ( P = 0.8) ( Figure 1 ).

evidence.title: Comparative analysis of GPT-4-based ChatGPT's diagnostic performance with radiologists using real-world radiology reports of brain tumors
evidence.outcome: Diagnostic accuracy of GPT-4 versus neuroradiologists and general radiologists on same report text
evidence.effect: GPT-4 final diagnostic accuracy 73% vs radiologists 65-79%; differential diagnosis accuracy 94% vs radiologists 73-89%.
evidence.quote: In a study analyzing 150 radiological reports, GPT-4 achieved a final diagnostic accuracy of 73%, while radiologists' accuracy ranged from 65 to 79%.
evidence.sample_unit: radiology reports (brain MRI, preoperative brain tumor patients)

evidence.title: Psychosis metabolic risk calculator (PsyMetRiC) in early psychosis: External validation study in Finland
evidence.outcome: Discrimination and net benefit of PsyMetRiC compared with FINDRISC on same data
evidence.effect: C-statistic 0.72 (full) and 0.70 (partial) vs 0.63 for FINDRISC; at 15% threshold net benefit 0.13 for PsyMetRiC-Fi vs 0.01 for FINDRISC.
evidence.quote: Both PsyMetRiC versions showed superior discriminative accuracy in this early psychosis population compared with using FINDRISC.

evidence.title: Comparison of AI-integrated pathways with human-AI interaction in population mammographic screening for breast cancer
evidence.outcome: AI reader and AI-integrated pathways compared with radiologists and standard of care on same data
evidence.effect: AI standalone sensitivity 75.0 vs 66.3% for mean individual radiologist; reader-replacement achieved 82.3% sensitivity and 96.3% specificity vs standard of care 79.8%/96.0%.
evidence.quote: The AI reader-replacement scenario produced higher system sensitivity (82.3%; 95% CI 81.5–83.1, P < 0.0025) and higher specificity (96.3%; 95% CI 96.2–96.3, P < 4.3 × 10 −6 ) than the current standard of care system (Fig. 3 A and Supplementary Table 2 ).

evidence.title: Retrieving Evidence from EHRs with LLMs: Possibilities and Challenges
evidence.outcome: Expert preference for LLM-based retrieval versus pre-LLM information retrieval baseline
evidence.effect: LLM-based approach provides outputs consistently preferred to a pre-LLM information retrieval baseline under expert evaluation.
evidence.quote: Under expert evaluation, we find that this LLM-based approach provides outputs consistently preferred to a pre-LLM information retrieval baseline.

evidence.title: AI-integrated Screening to Replace Double Reading of Mammograms: A Population-wide Accuracy and Feasibility Study
evidence.outcome: performance versus standard double reading
evidence.effect: AIfirst no accuracy difference except arbitration +0.99%; AIsecond sensitivity −1.58%; AItriage sensitivity +1.33%, PPV +0.36%, NPV +0.01%.
evidence.quote: Replacing one or both readers with AI seems feasible; however, the site of application in the workflow can have clinically relevant effects on accuracy and workload.

evidence.title: Enhancing Patient Selection in Sepsis Clinical Trials Design Through an AI Enrichment Strategy: Algorithm Development and Validation
evidence.outcome: candidate model comparison
evidence.effect: GBM had highest persistent-ill AUROC range, 0.806-0.807, versus NDF 0.779-0.802, RF 0.791-0.795, and LR 0.719-0.790.
evidence.quote: Of the 4 machine learning architectures in 3 model setups for predicting persistent ill on internal validation, GBM had the highest consistent performance of mean AUROC (SD) ranging from 0.806 (0.010) to 0.807 (0.010) compared to NDF ranging from 0.779 (0.013) to 0.802 (0.011), RF ranging from 0.791 (0.013) to 0.795 (0.010), and LR ranging from 0.719 (0.031) to 0.790 (0.007; Multimedia Appendix 6 ).
evidence.sample_unit: patients with sepsis (9135 MIMIC-IV development; 3743 eICU-CRD external validation)

evidence.title: External Validation Demonstrates Machine Learning Models Outperform Human Experts in Prediction of Objective and Patient-reported Overactive Bladder Treatment Outcomes
evidence.outcome: AUC of ML models versus human experts and other algorithms in external validation set
evidence.effect: Operator splitting neural network AUC 0.66 vs XGBoost 0.58, logistic regression 0.55, human experts 0.47-0.53 for clinical responder status; patient-reported improvement AUC 0.64 vs experts 0.41-0.62.
evidence.quote: In the validation set, the operator splitting neural network had AUC of 0.66 and outperformed XGBoost with DART (top available machine-learning classifier, AUC: 0.58), logistic regression (AUC 0.55), and human experts (AUC 0.47-0.53) for prediction of clinical responder status.

evidence.title: Clinical utility of an artificial intelligence radiomics-based tool for risk stratification of pulmonary nodules
evidence.outcome: Predictive accuracy of Mayo clinical model with vs without AI LCP score
evidence.effect: AUC 0.58 (Mayo) vs 0.65 (Mayo + LCP); likelihood ratio P = .012; sensitivity 56% vs 38% at 65% threshold; standardized net benefit 18% vs -3.3%
evidence.quote: At the 65% risk threshold, the Mayo + LCP model was associated with increased sensitivity (56% vs 38%; P = .019), similar false positive rate (33% vs 35%; P = .8), and increased standardized net benefit (18% vs -3.3%) compared with the Mayo model.

evidence.title: Comparing the Ability of Google and ChatGPT to Accurately Respond to Oculoplastics-Related Patient Questions and Generate Customized Oculoplastics Patient Education Materials
evidence.outcome: FAQ accuracy and preference versus Google
evidence.effect: ChatGPT: 93% accuracy vs Google: 78% (p < 0.001); preferred by panelists 79%.
evidence.quote: ChatGPT responses (93% accuracy) were significantly more accurate (p < 0.001) than Google responses (78% accuracy) and were preferred by expert panelists (79%).
evidence.sample_unit: patient FAQs (10 oculoplastics conditions) plus 8 procedure explanations

evidence.title: Establishing a novel score system and using it to assess and compare the quality of ChatGPT-4 consultation with physician consultation for obstetrics and gynecology: A pilot study
evidence.venue: International journal of gynaecology and obstetrics: the official organ of the International Federation of Gynaecology and Obstetrics
evidence.outcome: Consultation quality score of ChatGPT-4 versus physicians on the same cases
evidence.effect: Physician consultation scores were significantly higher than ChatGPT-4 in both obstetric and gynecologic patients; agreement between the two was unacceptable and correlation weak or absent.
evidence.quote: Paired t tests showed that the scores of physician consultations were significantly higher than those generated by ChatGPT-4 in both obstetric and gynecologic patients.

evidence.title: Comparison of NLP machine learning models with human physicians for ASA Physical Status classification
evidence.outcome: NLP model performance versus board-certified anesthesiologists on ASA-PS classification, same test data
evidence.effect: ClinicalBigBird AUROC 0.915; specificity 0.901 vs 0.897, precision 0.732 vs 0.715, F1 0.716 vs 0.713 compared with anesthesiologists (all p<0.01).
evidence.quote: It outperformed board-certified anesthesiologists with a specificity of 0.901 vs. 0.897, precision of 0.732 vs. 0.715, and F1-score of 0.716 vs. 0.713 (all p <0.01).

evidence.title: Artificial intelligence based real-time prediction of imminent heart failure hospitalisation in patients undergoing non-invasive telemedicine
evidence.outcome: ROC AUC of ML risk score versus conventional heuristic algorithm on the same data
evidence.effect: ML model outperformed the conventional algorithm: ROCAUC 0.855 vs. 0.727, p < 0.001.
evidence.quote: The machine learning model significantly outperformed the conventional algorithm (ROCAUC 0.855 vs. 0.727, p < 0.001).

evidence.title: Evaluating the use of large language models to provide clinical recommendations in the Emergency Department
evidence.outcome: LLM accuracy versus resident physician on admission, radiology, and antibiotic recommendations
evidence.effect: GPT-4-turbo and GPT-3.5-turbo accuracy 8% and 24% lower than the resident physician on average; LLMs overly cautious, high sensitivity at cost of specificity.
evidence.quote: We found that both GPT-4-turbo and GPT-3.5-turbo performed poorly compared to a resident physician, with accuracy scores 8% and 24%, respectively, lower than physician on average.

evidence.title: Performance of Machine Learning Suicide Risk Models in an American Indian Population
evidence.outcome: ML models compared with existing screening on the same local data (AUROC)
evidence.effect: 90-day attempt AUROC: MHRN 0.81, VU 0.68, existing screening 0.66; screening identified no suicide deaths (sensitivity 0.0%) while MHRN AUROC for death was 0.86.
evidence.quote: Our results show that the machine learning models used in this study had substantially higher AUROC values than existing approaches, even when compared with a substantial uptick in ASQ administration (eTable 5 in Supplement 1 ).

evidence.title: Early Warning Scores With and Without Artificial Intelligence
evidence.outcome: Discrimination of AI early warning scores versus simpler non-AI scores for clinical deterioration on the same data
evidence.effect: eCART AUROC 0.895 (95% CI 0.891-0.900) vs NEWS2 0.831, NEWS 0.829, RI 0.828, EDI 0.808, MEWS 0.757; NEWS, a non-AI score, significantly outperformed EDI.
evidence.quote: In this cohort study of inpatient encounters, eCART outperformed the other AI and non-AI scores, identifying more deteriorating patients with fewer false alarms and sufficient time to intervene.

evidence.title: GPT-4-based AI agents-the new expert system for detection of antimicrobial resistance mechanisms?
evidence.outcome: Concordance and specificity of GPT-agent versus microbiologists against routine diagnostics
evidence.effect: Microbiologists concordant in 94.4% of categories vs 81.9% for EUCAST-GPT-expert; humans had higher specificities (ESBL 99.1% vs 69.23%).
evidence.quote: Microbiologists showed higher concordance and shorter argumentations compared to GPT-agents.

evidence.title: Grading of diabetic retinopathy using a pre-segmenting deep learning classification model: Validation of an automated algorithm
evidence.outcome: Autonomous DL algorithm performance compared with certified human grader against gold standard
evidence.effect: Weighted kappa 0.72 (DL) vs 0.88 (human); sensitivity 78% vs 95%; specificity 81% vs 82%; NPV at 23.8% prevalence 92% vs 98%.
evidence.quote: In this validation study of an autonomous pre‐segmenting DR classification DL algorithm tested in a high‐risk real‐world population, the findings revealed that the stand‐alone AI model had a comparable specificity but a lower sensitivity when compared to a certified human grader either acting with or without assistance from the DL algorithm.

evidence.title: Evaluation of the Appropriateness and Readability of ChatGPT-4 Responses to Patient Queries on Uveitis
evidence.outcome: Specialist ratings versus existing patient-education websites
evidence.effect: Standard ChatGPT-4 preference 4.37–4.59 vs websites 2.90–3.45; comprehensiveness 4.40–4.78 vs 2.00–3.13; accuracy similar, all P>0.05.
evidence.quote: It was found that trained specialists preferred the standard responses provided by ChatGPT-4, and perceived these responses to be more comprehensive while maintaining accuracy compared with contents from the existing websites ( Table 3 ).

evidence.title: Large language models can support generation of standardized discharge summaries - A retrospective study utilizing ChatGPT-4 and electronic health records
evidence.outcome: Blinded specialist quality ratings of AI-generated vs resident-written discharge summaries
evidence.effect: Human DS rated higher than AI (mean 3.78 vs 3.12, p<0.05); humans surpassed AI in 12/15 questions and 16/20 cases; favored by 7/8 raters.
evidence.quote: Human-written DS were rated significantly higher than AI (mean ratings: human 3.78, AI 3.12, p < 0.05).

evidence.title: Development and assessment of a machine learning tool for predicting emergency admission in Scotland
evidence.outcome: Discrimination and calibration of new emergency admission score versus previously deployed scores
evidence.effect: Improvements in discrimination and calibration over previous scores deployed in Scotland, with stability over a 3-year timeframe (no numbers in abstract)
evidence.quote: We demonstrate improvements in discrimination and calibration with respect to previous scores deployed in Scotland, as well as stability over a 3-year timeframe.

evidence.title: Strategies for integrating artificial intelligence into mammography screening programmes: a retrospective simulation analysis
evidence.outcome: AI integration strategies versus radiologist double-reading screening programme on cancer detection rate, recall, workload
evidence.effect: Standalone AI achieved non-inferior CDR 6.37 vs programme 6.32 per 1000, recall 3.80 vs 4.11 per 100; decision referral CDR 6.85, recall 3.55, 84% workload reduction.
evidence.quote: Compared with the German screening programme (CDR 6·32 per 1000 examinations, recall rate 4·11 per 100 examinations), replacement of both readers (standalone AI strategy) achieved a non-inferior CDR of 6·37 (95% CI 6·10-6·64) at a recall rate of 3·80 (95% CI 3·67-3·93), whereas single reader replacement achieved a CDR of 6·49 (6·31-6·67), a recall rate of 4·01 (3·92-4·10), and a 49% workload reduction.
evidence.sample_unit: screening examinations (Germany n=1,657,068; UK n=223,603; Sweden n=22,779)

evidence.title: Enhancing Coronary Revascularization Decisions: The Promising Role of Large Language Models as a Decision-Support Tool for Multidisciplinary Heart Team
evidence.outcome: Concordance of LLM revascularization recommendations with multidisciplinary heart team decisions on the same cases
evidence.effect: ChatGPT-4: accuracy 0.82, sensitivity 0.8, specificity 0.83, kappa 0.59; ChatGPT-3.5: 0.67, 0.27, 0.84, 0.12. Model versions differed substantially.
evidence.quote: ChatGPT-4 showed high concordance with decisions made by the MDHT (accuracy 0.82, sensitivity 0.8, specificity 0.83, and kappa 0.59), while ChatGPT-3.5 (0.67, 0.27, 0.84, and 0.12, respectively) showed lower concordance.

evidence.title: Diagnostic Accuracy of Automated Diabetic Retinopathy Image Assessment Software: IDx-DR and RetCAD
evidence.outcome: Head-to-head diagnostic accuracy of two competing AI DR screening products on the same cohort
evidence.effect: IDx-DR sensitivity 99.3%, specificity 68.9%; RetCAD sensitivity 89.4%, specificity 94.8%. PPV 48.1% vs 96.4%; NPV 99.5% vs 83.1%. Operating trade-offs differed materially between products.
evidence.quote: In this direct comparison using the same patient cohort, the two algorithms showed differences in their operating parameters for RDR screening.

evidence.title: Performance of ChatGPT on prehospital acute ischemic stroke and large vessel occlusion (LVO) stroke screening
evidence.outcome: Comparison of GPT-4 versus GPT-3.5 (and prehospital scales) on stroke and LVO screening on same records
evidence.effect: GPT-4 outperformed GPT-3.5 in AIS (AUC 0.75 vs 0.59, P=0.015) and LVO (AUC 0.71 vs 0.60, P<0.001); results comparable to prehospital scales.
evidence.quote: GPT-4 outperformed GPT-3.5 in AIS screening (AUC 0.75 (0.65-0.84) vs 0.59 (0.50-0.69), P = 0.015) and LVO identification (AUC 0.71 (0.65-0.77) vs 0.60 (0.53-0.66), P < 0.001).

evidence.title: Collaboration between clinicians and vision-language models in radiology report generation
evidence.outcome: Radiologist panel preference for AI-generated versus clinician-written chest X-ray reports on the same cases
evidence.effect: 56.1% of ICU AI reports preferable or equivalent to clinician reports by half or more of panel; 77.7% for in/outpatient overall; 94% for cases with no pertinent abnormal findings.
evidence.quote: We observe a wide distribution of preferences across the panel and across clinical settings, with 56.1% of Flamingo-CXR intensive care reports evaluated to be preferable or equivalent to clinician reports, by half or more of the panel, rising to 77.7% for in/outpatient X-rays overall and to 94% for the subset of cases with no pertinent abnormal findings.

evidence.title: OSAIRIS: Lessons Learned From the Hospital-Based Implementation and Evaluation of an Open-Source Deep-Learning Model for Radiotherapy Image Segmentation
evidence.venue: Clinical oncology (Royal College of Radiologists (Great Britain))
evidence.outcome: blinded contour ratings
evidence.effect: Gold standard clinician contours were not rated more highly than AI-generated contours.
evidence.quote: Notably, our blinded clinician contour rating exercise showed that gold standard clinician contours are not rated more highly than the AI-generated contours.

evidence.title: A Novel Management Challenge in Age-Related Macular Degeneration: Artificial Intelligence and Expert Prediction of Geographic Atrophy
evidence.outcome: AI versus ophthalmologists on GA progression prediction accuracy, kappa, and c-index on the same eyes
evidence.effect: Humans: accuracy 0.37-0.43, κ 0.06-0.18, c-index 0.59-0.62. AI (OCT only): accuracy 0.48, κ 0.23, c-index 0.69.
evidence.quote: Automated AI-based analysis reached an accuracy of 0.48 and κ of 0.23 on the first task, and c-index of 0.69 on the second task solely utilizing OCT imaging.

evidence.title: Stratified Care in Cognitive Behavioural Therapy: A Comparative Evaluation of Predictive Modelling Approaches for Individualized Treatment: La stratification des soins pour l'orientation vers une thérapie cognitivo-comportementale: une évaluation comparative des approches de modélisation prédictive pour un traitement individualisé
evidence.venue: Canadian journal of psychiatry. Revue canadienne de psychiatrie
evidence.outcome: Accuracy of model-derived treatment intensity assignment versus clinician-assigned intensity against actual case complexity
evidence.effect: Both model cut-offs had higher accuracy than clinician assignment (clinician .590; 0.5 cut-off .690; ROC cut-off .749).
evidence.quote: Both predictive model cut-offs demonstrated higher accuracy than the clinician-assigned treatment intensities, achieving the highest accuracy (.749) using the ROC cut-off point.

evidence.title: The Treasure Trove Hidden in Plain Sight: The Utility of GPT-4 in Chest Radiograph Evaluation
evidence.outcome: GPT-4 ADA ML model AUC and accuracy versus human specialist-developed reference models on same data
evidence.quote: ML strategies were valid and based on consistent coding routines, resulting in valid outputs on par with human specialist-developed reference models (AUC, 0.80 [95% CI: 0.80, 0.81] vs 0.80 [95% CI: 0.80, 0.81]; P = .51) (accuracy, 79% [6910 of 8758 patients] vs 78% [6875 of 8758 patients], respectively; P = .27).

evidence.title: How soon will surgeons become mere technicians? Chatbot performance in managing clinical scenarios
evidence.venue: The Journal of thoracic and cardiovascular surgery
evidence.outcome: Chatbot vs board-certified surgeon scores on board-style thoracic surgery scenarios
evidence.effect: Median score per scenario was 1.06 for chatbots vs 1.88 for surgeons (difference 0.66; P = .019); chatbots were worse in all but 2 scenarios.
evidence.quote: The median score per scenario was 1.06 for chatbots, compared to 1.88 for surgeons (difference, 0.66; P = .019).
evidence.sample_unit: clinical scenarios (each answered by 4 chatbots and 21 board-certified thoracic surgeons)

evidence.title: Deep Learning Algorithms for Breast Cancer Detection in a UK Screening Cohort: As Stand-alone Readers and Combined with Human Readers
evidence.outcome: stand-alone AI versus single reader
evidence.effect: Two of three stand-alone algorithms achieved noninferior sensitivity; sensitivities 64.8%, 56.7%, 58.9% vs first reader 62.8%; specificities 92.8%, 96.8%, 97.9% vs 96.5%.
evidence.quote: Two of three stand-alone DL algorithms achieved noninferior sensitivity (DL-1: 64.8%, P < .001; DL-2: 56.7%, P = .03; DL-3: 58.9%, P < .001) compared with the single first reader (62.8%), and specificity was noninferior for DL-1 (92.8%; P < .001) and DL-2 (96.8%; P < .001) and superior for DL-3 (97.9%; P < .001) compared with the single first reader (96.5%).

evidence.title: Using Large Language Models to Abstract Complex Social Determinants of Health From Original and Deidentified Medical Notes: Development and Validation Study
evidence.outcome: Comparison of GPT-4, GPT-3.5, NER model, RegEx and manual abstraction on same notes
evidence.effect: GPT-4 had highest performance among automated methods with higher recall than humans (0.924 vs 0.702) but lower precision (0.850 vs 0.971).
evidence.quote: GPT-4 outperformed GPT-3.5, JSL, and RegEx in identifying patients experiencing current or past housing instability.
evidence.sample_unit: manually abstracted clinical notes (from 355 pregnant patients)

evidence.title: Efficacy of Early Warning Scores as the Prediction Tool for Detecting Patients With Acute Deterioration in a High Dependent Unit
evidence.outcome: Composite outcome prediction
evidence.quote: The AUC for NEWS was significantly superior to that of VSI for the composite outcome (p=0.014).

evidence.title: Artificial intelligence-assisted delineation for postoperative radiotherapy in patients with lung cancer: a prospective, multi-center, cohort study
evidence.outcome: OAR contouring accuracy versus clinicians
evidence.effect: AI-assisted OAR DSC was >0.8; left/right lungs, heart, and liver DSC >0.9; all P<0.05 versus manual contours.
evidence.quote: Additionally, the accuracy of the AI-assisted delineation significantly outperformed fully manual contours by junior radiation oncologists, with DSC greater than 0.8, among which the left and right lungs, heart and liver performed better, with DSC greater than 0.9 (all P< 0.05).

evidence.title: Evaluating the dosimetric impact of deep-learning-based auto-segmentation in prostate cancer radiotherapy: Insights into real-world clinical implementation and inter-observer variability
evidence.venue: Journal of applied clinical medical physics
evidence.outcome: Geometric and dosimetric agreement of AI contours versus original and expert manual contours
evidence.effect: AC-vs-manual geometric differences were smaller than manual-vs-manual for bladder and femoral heads; IMRT PTV D95 77.62±0.38 Gy (AC) vs 77.58±0.69 (OC) and 77.71±0.53 (EC); contouring time 0.53 vs 24.9 min.
evidence.quote: Our automated contouring system can reduce inter-expert variability and achieve dosimetric accuracy comparable to gold standard reference contours, highlighting its potential for streamlining clinical workflows.

evidence.title: The analytical and clinical validity of AI algorithms to score TILs in TNBC: can we use different machine learning models interchangeably?
evidence.outcome: Comparison of ten AI TIL models on analytical and prognostic validity against invasive disease-free survival
evidence.effect: Analytical validity differed across models (Spearman's r = 0.63-0.73, p < 0.001); eight of ten models were prognostic with overlapping HR = 0.40-0.47 (p < 0.004) in external cohort.
evidence.quote: A significant difference in analytical validity (Spearman's r = 0.63-0.73, p < 0.001) is highlighted across AI methodologies and training strategies.
evidence.sample_unit: patients (79 Yale analytical/development cohort; 215 Swedish prognostic validation cohort)

evidence.title: Development and validation of a deep learning pipeline to diagnose ovarian masses using ultrasound screening: a retrospective multicenter study
evidence.outcome: AI diagnostic performance compared with senior radiologists on the same external video data
evidence.effect: OvaMTA AUC 0.911 on 159 videos, comparable to senior radiologists (ACC 86.2 vs 88.1, p=0.50; SEN 81.8 vs 88.6, p=0.16; SPE 89.2 vs 87.6, p=0.68).
evidence.quote: In video-based external testing, OvaMTA recognised 159 videos with ovarian masses with AUC of 0.911, and is comparable to the performance of senior radiologists (ACC: 86.2 vs. 88.1, p = 0.50; SEN: 81.8 vs. 88.6, p = 0.16; SPE: 89.2 vs. 87.6, p = 0.68).

evidence.title: EyeGPT for Patient Inquiries and Medical Education: Development and Validation of an Ophthalmology Large Language Model
evidence.outcome: EyeGPT answers compared with unassisted ophthalmologists across four dimensions
evidence.effect: EyeGPT ranked best more often for understandability (19.2% vs 10%) and empathy (34.2% vs 6.7%) but slightly lower for accuracy (10% vs 11.7%) and trustworthiness (10% vs 12.5%).
evidence.quote: however, the accuracy and trustworthiness of EyeGPT answers were slightly lower than those by the ophthalmologists (accuracy: 12/120, 10% vs 14/120, 11.7%; trustworthiness: 12/120, 10% vs 15/120, 12.5%), highlighting areas for improvement.

evidence.title: Evaluating Large Language Model-Supported Instructions for Medication Use: First Steps Toward a Comprehensive Model
evidence.outcome: Comparison of GPT-4 versus Llama 3 output adequacy and errors on same scenarios
evidence.effect: Adequacy comparable (P=.818); hallucinations more frequent with Llama 3 than GPT-4 (8.7% vs 1.0%, P=.008); Llama 3 had fewer task-response errors (P=.001).
evidence.quote: However, hallucinations or incorrect information (error type 7) was more frequent in texts generated by Llama 3 than in those generated by GPT-4 (8.7% vs 1.0%, P =.008, respectively).

evidence.title: Comparative Analysis of M4CXR, an LLM-Based Chest X-Ray Report Generation Model, and ChatGPT in Radiological Interpretation
evidence.outcome: Comparison of specialized CXR model versus general-purpose ChatGPT-4o on the same images
evidence.effect: M4CXR outperformed ChatGPT across all metrics; anatomical localization accuracy 76-77.5% vs 36-36.5%; diagnostic acceptability 60-62% vs 42-45%.
evidence.quote: M4CXR showed better performance in anatomical localization (76-77.5% accuracy) compared to ChatGPT (36-36.5%) and demonstrated fewer instances of hallucination.

evidence.title: Evaluating Artificial Intelligence-Driven Responses to Acute Liver Failure Queries: A Comparative Analysis Across Accuracy, Clarity, and Relevance
evidence.outcome: Comparison of five LLMs and RAG-enhanced GPT-4 on the same ALF questions
evidence.effect: GPT-4+RAG scored highest (4.70, 4.89, 4.78); BARD scored 2.01 accuracy and COPILOT 2.26 accuracy, showing large differences between candidate tools.
evidence.quote: Meanwhile, BARD and COPILOT exhibited lower performance levels; BARD recorded scores of 2.01 in accuracy and 3.03 in relevance, while COPILOT obtained 2.26 in accuracy and 3.12 in relevance.

evidence.title: Development, validation and recalibration of a prediction model for prediabetes: an EHR and NHANES-based study
evidence.venue: BMC medical informatics and decision making
evidence.outcome: LASSO versus approximation discrimination
evidence.effect: Optimism-corrected C-statistics were 0.760 for LASSO and 0.763 for approximation.
evidence.quote: Both the LASSO and approximation models demonstrated similar discrimination in the EHR cohort, with optimism-corrected C-statistics of 0.760 and 0.763, respectively.
evidence.sample_unit: patients (EHR development cohort); 2,348 NHANES participants for external validation

evidence.title: Enhancing AI reliability: A foundation model with uncertainty estimation for optical coherence tomography-based retinal disease diagnosis
evidence.outcome: F1 score of AI versus clinicians and GPT-4V on OCT diagnosis
evidence.effect: FMUE F1 96.30% vs retinal experts 86.95% (p=0.004), senior doctors 82.71%, junior doctors 66.55%, GPT-4V 32.39% (all p<0.001).
evidence.quote: In human-model comparison, FMUE achieves a higher F1 score of 96.30% than retinal experts (86.95%, p = 0.004), senior doctors (82.71%, p < 0.001), junior doctors (66.55%, p < 0.001), and generative pretrained transformer 4 with vision (GPT-4V) (32.39%, p < 0.001).

evidence.title: Evaluating LLM-based generative AI tools in emergency triage: A comparative study of ChatGPT Plus, Copilot Pro, and triage nurses
evidence.venue: The American journal of emergency medicine
evidence.outcome: Triage accuracy of LLMs compared with triage nurses against EM physician reference
evidence.effect: Overall accuracy 65.2% nurses, 66.5% ChatGPT, 61.8% Copilot; Cohen's Kappa 0.537 ChatGPT, 0.477 nurses, 0.472 Copilot.
evidence.quote: The overall triage accuracy was 65.2 % for nurses, 66.5 % for ChatGPT, and 61.8 % for Copilot, with no significant difference (p = 0.000).

evidence.title: The Transformative Potential of Large Language Models in Mining Electronic Health Records Data: Content Analysis
evidence.outcome: LLM performance versus specialist physicians on comorbidity extraction from the same reports
evidence.effect: GPT-3.5 slightly lower than physicians (McNemar P=.79); GPT-4 superior on key metrics (P<.001), sensitivity 96.8% vs 88.8% for physicians; physicians marginally better precision (97.7% vs 96.8%).
evidence.quote: GPT-4 demonstrated clear superiority in several key metrics (McNemar test, P<.001).

evidence.title: International multicenter validation of AI-driven ultrasound detection of ovarian cancer
evidence.outcome: AI diagnostic performance compared with expert and non-expert examiners on same data
evidence.effect: AI significantly outperformed both expert and non-expert examiners on all evaluated metrics; triage simulation reduced expert referrals by 63% while surpassing current practice.
evidence.quote: Furthermore, in a retrospective triage simulation, artificial intelligence (AI)-driven diagnostic support reduced referrals to experts by 63% while significantly surpassing the diagnostic performance of the current practice.

evidence.title: Validation of a Visual Field Prediction Tool for Glaucoma: A Multicenter Study Involving Patients With Glaucoma in the United Kingdom
evidence.outcome: Comparison of the AI model against conventional linear regression standard on same data
evidence.effect: PKF 75.7% within 2.5 dB at 60 months vs LR models substantially lower (P<.01); 95% repeatability interval proportion 67.9% vs 40.2% and 40.9%.
evidence.quote: The proportion of MD predictions in the 95% repeatability intervals at 60 months' follow-up for PKF (67.9%) was higher than those for the LR models (40.2%, 40.9%) and similar to that for UK-KF (71.4%).

evidence.title: Prospective Multi-Site Validation of AI to Detect Tuberculosis and Chest X-Ray Abnormalities
evidence.outcome: TB AI sensitivity/specificity vs ten radiologists on same CXRs
evidence.effect: High-sensitivity threshold: AI 87% sens/70% spec vs radiologists 76%/82%; noninferior for sensitivity (P<0.001), not specificity (P=0.99). Balanced threshold 78%/82%, comparable to radiologists.
evidence.quote: At the high-sensitivity threshold, the TB AI was noninferior to average radiologist sensitivity (P<0.001) but not to average radiologist specificity (P=0.99) and was higher than the WHO target for specificity but not sensitivity.

evidence.title: Can ChatGPT 4.0 Diagnose Epilepsy? A Study on Artificial Intelligence's Diagnostic Capabilities
evidence.outcome: Agreement and diagnostic accuracy of ChatGPT 4.0 versus epileptologists for epilepsy diagnosis
evidence.effect: Cohen's kappa -0.01 (95% CI -0.08 to 0.06); sensitivity 17.6%, specificity 81.4%; errors in 41.7% of cases; epilepsy diagnosed in 18.2% by ChatGPT vs 36.2% by neurologists.
evidence.quote: ChatGPT 4.0 does not reach human clinicians' performance in diagnosing epilepsy, showing poor performance in identifying epilepsy but better at recognizing non-epileptic cases.

evidence.title: A deep learning model for carotid plaques detection based on CTA images: a two stepwise early-stage clinical validation study
evidence.outcome: Model diagnostic performance compared against 6 radiologists on the same plaque cases
evidence.effect: Model diagnostic results were higher than those of 4 out of 6 radiologists (p < 0.001). Model diagnostic time was 6 s, significantly shorter than that of all radiologists (p < 0.001).
evidence.quote: Especially, in the clinical application scenario analysis, the model's diagnostic results for plaques were found to be higher than those of 4 out of 6 radiologists (p < 0.001).

evidence.title: Large-Scale Validation of the Feasibility of GPT-4 as a Proofreading Tool for Head CT Reports
evidence.outcome: Error detection sensitivity and review time of GPT-4 versus human radiologist readers on same reports
evidence.effect: Human readers had worse factual error detection sensitivity (0.33-0.69 vs 0.89) and took longer (82-121 s vs 16 s, P<.001) than GPT-4.
evidence.quote: Compared with GPT-4, human readers had worse factual error detection sensitivity (0.33-0.69 vs 0.89; P = .008 for radiologist 4, P < .001 for others) and took longer to review (82-121 seconds vs 16 seconds, P < .001).

evidence.title: A phenotype-based AI pipeline outperforms human experts in differentially diagnosing rare diseases using EHRs
evidence.outcome: Top-3 and top-10 recall of AI versus specialist physicians, LLMs, and 13 prediction methods
evidence.effect: Top-3 recall 0.613 and top-10 recall 0.813 in 75 cases, surpassing 50 specialists, ChatGPT and GPT-4; 0.513/0.654 in 1936 test cases surpassing 13 methods.
evidence.quote: In a human-computer study with 75 cases, PhenoBrain exhibited exceptional performance with a top-3 recall of 0.613 and a top-10 recall of 0.813, surpassing the performance of 50 specialist physicians and large language models like ChatGPT and GPT-4.

evidence.title: Exploring potential drug-drug interactions in discharge prescriptions: ChatGPT's effectiveness in assessing those interactions
evidence.venue: Exploratory research in clinical and social pharmacy
evidence.outcome: ChatGPT-4.0 pDDI prediction compared with Micromedex checker on the same discharge prescriptions
evidence.effect: ChatGPT matched Micromedex for interaction occurrence (100%) but had limited accuracy for severity (37.3%) and moderate accuracy for onset (65.2%).
evidence.quote: ChatGPT-4.0 accurately identified pDDIs (100 % for occurrence) but had limited accuracy for severity (37.3 %) and moderate accuracy for onset (65.2 %).

evidence.title: Leveraging Large Language Models to Generate Clinical Histories for Oncologic Imaging Requisitions
evidence.outcome: LLM-generated vs original physician requisition histories: completeness, quality, radiologist preference, perceived harm
evidence.effect: LLM histories more often included primary diagnosis (99.5% vs 89%), acute symptoms (15% vs 4%), surgery (61% vs 12%); radiologists preferred LLM histories 89% vs 5%; lower likelihood of harm 3% vs 55%.
evidence.quote: Compared with original requisition histories, LLM-generated histories were more complete and were preferred by radiologists for imaging interpretation and perceived safety.

evidence.title: Validation of an Artificial Intelligence-Powered Virtual Assistant for Emergency Triage in Neurology
evidence.outcome: Virtual assistant diagnostic and safety performance versus ChatGPT 3.5 and 4, rated by neurologists
evidence.effect: VA superior to both ChatGPT versions in all evaluated diagnostic and safety aspects (P<0.0001).
evidence.quote: VA showed superiority over both versions of ChatGPT in all evaluated diagnostic and safety aspects ( P <0.0001).

evidence.title: Smart Pharmaceutical Monitoring System With Personalized Medication Schedules and Self-Management Programs for Patients With Diabetes: Development and Evaluation Study
evidence.outcome: Head-to-head expert ratings of DUMS, pharmacist-refined output, and GPT-4 on same prescriptions
